bullets: Sir, this is the IT department. I manage Active Directory, not plumbing. I do not have a plunger. I have a keyboard.
"But you guys fix everything, right?" â€” no. We fix everything that plugs into a wall socket and runs electricity. We do not fix what plugs into the sewage line.
The plumber's number is on the same intranet page as the IT helpdesk number. Scroll down. It is right there.
Note: Calling IT for a blocked toilet will result in your ticket being assigned to /dev/urinal.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT BECAUSE THE TOILET IS LEAKING...

bullets: I manage the servers. I do not manage the supply cupboard. I do not know where the blue pens are.
"Can you order me a new chair?" â€” I can order you a new docking station. I cannot order you an ergonomic throne to sit on while you browse Facebook.
If you need staples, paper clips, or a new mug, call procurement. Their extension is literally one digit off from ours. Yes, we know. No, we will not transfer you for the fifth time.
Note: IT is not the general office admin department. We do not stock sticky notes.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK IT TO ORDER YOUR STATIONERY...

bullets: The server room AC is IT's responsibility because the servers will melt without it. Your office AC is facilities management's problem.
I cannot "just tweak the building thermostat from my computer." That is not a thing. I do not have magic climate control software.
"But it's 30 degrees in here and my laptop is overheating" â€” then take a break, go outside, and let facilities know. Do not call IT to complain about the weather inside your office.
Note: The AC being broken is uncomfortable. It is not an IT emergency. Unless the server room is 40 degrees, do not call us.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT BECAUSE THE AIR CONDITIONER IS BROKEN...

bullets: I support company-issued equipment. Your personal Dell that you bought in 2018 from Cash Converters is not covered by our support contract.
"Can you just take a quick look?" â€” no. Because "a quick look" becomes two hours of unpaid work, and then I am responsible for whatever happens next.
The company IT budget does not cover your son's gaming PC, your wife's MacBook, or your uncle's "computer that won't turn on."
Note: We do not offer "IT for the whole family" plans. We are not Telkom. We are the corporate IT department.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BRING YOUR PERSONAL LAPTOP TO IT FOR FREE REPAIRS...

bullets: The access control system falls under IT's umbrella. The physical door handle does not. If the handle is loose, call maintenance.
"My access card stopped working" â€” that is IT. "The door is stuck and I cannot push it open" â€” that is not IT.
We do not carry WD-40. We do not carry screwdrivers for hinges. We carry screwdrivers for server chassis. There is a difference.
Note: If it requires oil, it is not an IT problem. If it requires a reboot, it might be.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT BECAUSE THE OFFICE DOOR WON'T OPEN...

bullets: The coffee machine has a network connection for usage tracking. That network connection is IT's responsibility. The machine itself is not.
"The coffee machine is not working" â€” is it plugged in? Is the water reservoir full? Has it been descaled this century? These are not IT questions.
I do not know how to fix a coffee machine. I know how to fix a server. If I attempt to fix your coffee machine, you will not like the result.
Note: The coffee machine is not on our SLA. The printer is also not on our SLA, but we fix that anyway because we have given up fighting that battle.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT TO FIX THE COFFEE MACHINE...

bullets: Light switches exist. They are on the wall. They are not controlled by our server. We do not have a "lights" dashboard.
"The fluorescent tube in the ceiling is flickering" â€” replace the tube. That is not a DNS issue. I promise you.
If the building's power is out, that is Eskom. If the UPS is beeping, that is IT. If the overhead light is buzzing, that is facilities. Learn the difference.
Note: The only lights we control are the blinking ones on the network switches. The ceiling lights are not our jurisdiction.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT BECAUSE THE LIGHTS WON'T TURN ON...

bullets: The room says "capacity: 10 people." The TV screen is from 2012. The cable is VGA. Your laptop does not have VGA. You have just created a problem that cannot be solved in the 30 seconds before your meeting starts.
"There was an HDMI cable in the photo" â€” the photo was taken in 2019. The cable has since been stolen, lost, or chewed by the office dog. Do not trust the room photo.
A room booked for a video call with 14 participants requires a room that can seat 14 people. That is not the same room you use for a 3-person catch-up.
Note: Booking a room does not magically equip it with the technology you need. Check the inventory before you book.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BOOK A MEETING ROOM WITHOUT CHECKING THE TECH...

bullets: The five minutes of silence at the start of every meeting while someone says "can you hear me?" five times is not mandatory. It is avoidable.
Testing the microphone before the meeting takes 30 seconds. Those 30 seconds will save 5 minutes of fumbling and 10 minutes of "sorry, can you repeat that?"

"My audio is not working" â€” you are muted. You have been muted. The microphone icon has a red line through it. It has been like that since you joined. Everyone has been watching you talk to yourself.
Note: "Can you hear me?" is the most expensive phrase in corporate audio. Eliminate it from your vocabulary.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU START THE MEETING WITHOUT TESTING THE AUDIO...

bullets: The HDMI port is on the side of the laptop. Not the USB port. Not the Ethernet port. Not the charging port. The one that looks like a trapezoid with a hole in it.
If the cable does not fit, do not push harder. Pushing harder will not change the shape of the port. It will break the port.
There are adapters in the IT drawer. They are labelled. You walked past the IT drawer on the way to the meeting room. Stop pretending you did not see it.
Note: HDMI cables do not require physical force to insert. If you are struggling, you are doing it wrong. Stop and reconsider your life choices.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU STRUGGLE WITH THE HDMI CABLE FOR 10 MINUTES...

bullets: The Teams Room system is working perfectly. The camera is on. The microphone is receiving audio. The problem is that you are speaking from the far end of the table while looking at your laptop instead of the camera.
"The screen is not sharing" â€” you clicked "Share" but did not select which screen or window to share. The system is waiting for you. It will wait forever. It has patience. It is a machine.
"The call dropped" â€” the call dropped because someone in this room is on a VPN over Wi-Fi with a weak signal, not because the meeting room system is broken.
Note: Meeting room tech is not the enemy. It is a neutral party. The enemy is your refusal to learn how to use it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BLAME THE MEETING ROOM SYSTEM FOR A BAD MEETING...

bullets: The cables are configured in a specific layout to reach the table, connect to the screen, and provide enough slack for the laptop to sit comfortably. You unplugged them and now they do not reach.
"I just moved it slightly" â€” you rearranged the entire setup, threaded the cable behind the cabinet, and now it is tangled in the leg of the stand.
The USB extension cable that was taped to the table was taped there for a reason. You peeled it up. Now the cable falls behind the desk every time someone plugs in.
Note: If the cables were arranged a specific way, there was a reason. You are not a meeting room ergonomics specialist. Leave the cables alone.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU MOVE THE MEETING ROOM CABLES...

bullets: The previous meeting ended at 10:00. Your meeting starts at 10:00. The previous meeting ran over by 7 minutes. You are now standing outside the door waiting while 12 people slowly pack up their things.

The meeting room system needs 2 minutes between sessions to reset the connection and clear the cache. If you do not give it that time, the first 5 minutes of your meeting will be spent staring at someone else's leftovers on the screen.
"Can you kick the previous meeting out remotely?" â€” I can, but you will not like the phone call from their manager when the system cuts them off mid-presentation.
Note: Book a 30-minute slot for a 25-minute meeting. The buffer is not optional. It is survival.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BOOK BACK-TO-BACK MEETINGS IN THE SAME ROOM...

bullets: The conference phone has exactly three buttons: Answer, Hang Up, and Volume. You do not need a manual. You need to read the labels on the buttons.
"It's not connecting" â€” you pressed the wrong button. You pressed "Hold" instead of "Answer." The other party is on hold. They have been on hold for 4 minutes.
The phone is not "broken." It is "working exactly as designed but you are pressing the wrong buttons." There is a subtle difference.
Note: A device with three buttons is not complicated. The problem is not the device.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU COMPLAIN THAT THE CONFERENCE PHONE IS 'COMPLICATED'...

bullets: "The Cloud" is not a single magical place where all data floats eternally. It is someone else's server in a data centre in a specific country with a specific IP address.

If you saved your file to your desktop and then tell me "it should be in the cloud because we have OneDrive," you do not understand how OneDrive works. It syncs from specific folders. Your desktop may or may not be one of them.
"The Cloud lost my file" â€” the cloud did not lose it. You saved it somewhere you cannot find it. Search harder before submitting the ticket.
Note: The Cloud is not a backup strategy. It is a sync strategy. If you deleted it locally, it deleted from the cloud too. That is working as designed.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BLAME 'THE CLOUD' FOR YOUR MISSING FILES...

bullets: "The cloud" as a whole entity is not down. That would mean Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and every other provider simultaneously ceased to exist. That did not happen.
Your specific SaaS application may be experiencing an outage. That is not "the cloud." That is "the app." Two different things.

Before reporting "the cloud is down," check: Is your internet working? Can you open other websites? Have you tried turning it off and on again? If the answer to any of these is "no," the cloud is fine.
Note: "The cloud is down" is almost always "my internet is down" dressed up in fancier clothes.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'THE CLOUD IS DOWN'...

bullets: That project management tool you found, signed up for with your work email, and started using without going through procurement or security review is now a Shadow IT liability.
You agreed to terms of service that I have not reviewed. You stored company data on a server I do not control. You created a password that will be reused and leaked in the next data breach.
"But it was free!" â€” nothing is free. The product costs either your data, your privacy, or your compliance with regulations you did not know existed.
Note: Shadow IT is the enemy of security. If you want to use a new tool, ask first. If I say no, there is a reason.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SIGN UP FOR A SAAS PRODUCT WITHOUT TELLING IT...

bullets: You signed up for the enterprise plan with 500 users when you have 12 employees. You clicked "Upgrade" without reading the pricing page.
You added every single feature add-on, premium integration, and advanced analytics package because the buttons were green and inviting.
You forgot to cancel the free trial. It ended three months ago. The billing has been running every month. The amount is not a mistake. It is the consequence of your enthusiasm.
Note: Every SaaS free trial is designed to make you forget to cancel. The entire business model depends on it. Do not fall for it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK WHY YOUR SAAS BILL IS SO HIGH...

bullets: SharePoint is a document management system. It has folders, permissions, and version history. It works like a file server but with more steps.
"I cannot find my file" â€” you saved it to "General/Documents/Shared/Team/Archive/2024/Q4/Drafts/New Folder (3)/working_copy_final_v2.docx." That is a navigation problem, not a SharePoint problem.
"SharePoint deleted my file" â€” SharePoint did not delete it. You dragged it into a subfolder you did not know existed and now you cannot find it. Check the version history. It is still there.
Note: SharePoint is not complicated. Your filing system is chaotic. Organise your folders before you blame the platform.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU COMPLAIN THAT SHAREPOINT IS 'TOO COMPLICATED'...

bullets: Offline access requires you to sync the files to your local device before you board the flight. You cannot sync files while you are 30,000 feet in the air with no internet.
"But I need to work on the plane" â€” then sync the files before you leave for the airport. That is why the "Make Available Offline" button exists.
If you did not sync it before you lost internet, you do not have it. There is no secret cache in the sky that follows you around. The clue is in the name: "offline" access requires preparation.
Note: The cloud does not follow you into the sea, the mountains, or the air. Download your files before you leave civilization.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DEMAND 'OFFLINE ACCESS' TO YOUR CLOUD FILES...

bullets: Yes, because the office server is 10 metres away and the cloud server is potentially 1,000 kilometres away. The speed of light is fast but not instantaneous.
Your 20Mbps internet connection at home is not comparable to the 1Gbps fibre in the office. The cloud is not slow. Your internet is slow.
Also, the cloud is shared. If everyone in your building is streaming 4K Netflix at lunch, your SaaS application will respond accordingly. That is congestion, not cloud failure.
Note: The cloud is not magic. It runs on physical servers connected to physical cables. Physics applies.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLAIM 'THE CLOUD IS SLOWER THAN THE OFFICE SERVER'...

bullets: You are not a cybersecurity researcher. You are not doing us a favour. You are amplifying spam to 200 people who did not ask for it.
The "scam" you forwarded went to your entire address book including the CEO, the board, and that intern who started yesterday. They all now think you are a security risk.
If the email was truly dangerous, the security team already knows about it. They have a system. You are not part of it.
Note: Forwarding a phishing email to "everyone" does not make you a hero. It makes you the reason we have to send a "please ignore the previous email" follow-up.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU FORWARD THAT 'SCAM WARNING' TO THE ENTIRE COMPANY...

bullets: The IT department sent a fake phishing email to test your awareness. You not only clicked the link, but you also replied-all to the entire distribution list asking "Is this legitimate?"
You have now announced to 500 people that you failed the test. HR has a copy of the reply-all. Your manager has been notified.
The reply-all button is the most dangerous button in corporate email. Do not touch it. Ever. Under any circumstances. Pretend it does not exist.
Note: Replying-all to a phishing test is how you secure a mandatory re-training session. Congratulations.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REPLY-ALL TO A PHISHING TEST...

bullets: You did not win an iPhone. You have never won an iPhone. You will never win an iPhone from a pop-up ad on a streaming site.
The SMS that says "Your parcel is delayed" with a link that goes to a domain like "dhl-update-verification.xyz" is not from DHL. It is from a guy in a basement.
Clicking the link at 3 AM while half-asleep and entering your work email and password is not a mistake. It is a catastrophic lapse in judgment that will result in a compromised account.
Note: If it sounds too good to be true, it is a phishing attempt. If it sounds urgent and scary, it is also a phishing attempt. If it asks for your password, it is definitely a phishing attempt.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLICK 'YOU WON AN IPHONE' AT 3 AM...

bullets: The first thing you should do is disconnect your machine from the network. Do not call IT first. Disconnect first. Call second.
Yes, we know you clicked it. The security logs already flagged it. We were about to call you.
"I clicked it but I did not enter anything" â€” good. That is the best-case scenario. Still disconnect. Still report it. Still accept that we are going to run a full scan on your machine.
Note: Calling IT in a panic is fine. Calling IT after clicking the link and then doing nothing for 20 minutes while the payload installs is less fine.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT IN A PANIC AFTER CLICKING THE LINK...

bullets: That recipe website you signed up for in 2019 had a data breach. Your email and password are now on the dark web. Someone is currently trying that same password on your corporate email.
Password reuse is the single biggest security vulnerability in any organisation. Not the firewall. Not the antivirus. Your recycling of the same password across 47 different websites.
"But it is a strong password!" â€” it does not matter how strong it is if it was leaked in a breach and is now available for anyone to download.
Note: A password manager costs nothing. Reused passwords cost everything. Use unique passwords for every service. This is not optional.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REUSE YOUR WORK PASSWORD FOR PERSONAL SITES...

bullets: The security logs say you clicked. The timestamp matches your login session. The IP address matches your machine. You clicked.
"I do not remember clicking" â€” that is called autopilot. You were browsing without thinking. Your muscle memory betrayed you. It happens. But lying about it means I cannot help you.
If you admit you clicked, I can run the remediation and have you back online in 30 minutes. If you deny it, I have to treat your machine as fully compromised and rebuild it from scratch.
Note: "I did not click anything" is the most expensive lie in IT security. The truth is cheaper and faster.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLAIM 'I DID NOT CLICK ANYTHING'...

bullets: Every security prompt exists because someone before you did something catastrophic that required a new prompt to prevent.
MFA is not optional. It is the only thing standing between your email and a teenager in Lagos who wants to send spam from your account.
"But it takes an extra 10 seconds!" â€” restoring your identity after a breach takes 10 weeks. Choose which 10 you prefer to spend.
Note: Security is inconvenient by design. If it were convenient, it would not be secure.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'WHY DO WE NEED ALL THESE SECURITY PROMPTS?'...

bullets: The VPN encrypts all your traffic and routes it through the corporate network. That overhead costs about 10-15% of your bandwidth. That is not a bug. That is the price of security.

If you are connecting from a coffee shop with 5Mbps upload speed and complaining that the VPN is slow, the VPN is not the problem. Your decision to work from a location with dial-up speeds is the problem.
Streaming 4K YouTube while on the VPN and blaming the VPN for your laggy Teams calls is rich. The VPN is not the bottleneck. Your lack of bandwidth management is.
Note: The VPN does not make your internet slower. Your internet makes your VPN slower. Check your home connection before blaming the tunnel.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU COMPLAIN THAT THE VPN IS 'TOO SLOW'...

bullets: Working from a hammock looks idyllic on Instagram. In reality, your posture is destroyed, your laptop is overheating on your stomach, and your Wi-Fi signal is going through your body at a weird angle.
"My neck hurts from looking down at my screen" â€” that is ergonomics, not IT. I cannot prescribe you a chiropractor.
"My laptop keeps overheating" â€” it is on a soft fabric surface with no airflow. Of course it is overheating. Put it on a desk like a normal person.
Note: Working from a hammock, a bean bag, or your bed is not a technical problem. It is a life choice with consequences. Live with them.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU WORK FROM A HAMMOCK AND BLAME TECH...

bullets: The company issued you a laptop, not a home studio. If you want a multi-monitor setup for your spare bedroom, the company may provide it â€” but you have to ask properly, not demand it.
"I cannot work without two monitors" â€” you can. Millions of people do. You just do not want to. There is a difference.
If you are working from a kitchen counter with your laptop next to a toaster, a second monitor will not fix your workspace. A proper desk will.
Note: WFH equipment requests require a business justification, not a preference. "I want" is not a justification.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DEMAND A SECOND MONITOR FOR YOUR 'HOME OFFICE'...

bullets: Your microphone is picking up the coffee grinder, your neighbour's barking dog, and the construction site outside your window. Everyone on the call can hear it. They are all muted and judging you.
"Sorry, can you repeat that?" â€” I would love to, but I cannot hear you over the sound of your own blender.
Mute your microphone when you are not speaking. It is the single most important rule of video conferencing. Everything else is secondary.
Note: Joining a call from a public space with no headset is not "flexible working." It is "hostile audio." Invest in a microphone or invest in silence.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU JOIN A VIDEO CALL FROM A NOISY LOCATION...

bullets: There is a sticker over the camera lens. I can see it. You put it there for "privacy." Now you are complaining that the camera does not show your face.
A physical privacy shutter is not a defect. It is a feature. Slide it open and the camera will work exactly as designed.
"The camera is black" â€” because the lens cap is on. Remove the lens cap. I should not have to explain this.
Note: Webcams do not spontaneously stop working. They are covered, disabled, or disconnected. Check all three before calling IT.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLAIM YOUR WEBCAM 'DOES NOT WORK'...

bullets: Your home network is not part of the corporate infrastructure. I do not manage your Telkom router, your guests stealing your bandwidth, or your placement of the router behind a metal cabinet.
"The internet is slow" â€” have you tried rebooting your router? No? Then why are you calling me?
If you want a corporate-grade home network, the company may provide one. If you are using the free router your ISP gave you in 2016, you get what you pay for.
Note: WFH support covers the company laptop and the VPN. It does not cover your decision to put the router in the cupboard under the stairs.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK IT TO FIX YOUR HOME WI-FI...

bullets: Your personal laptop has no antivirus, no firewall, and no IT oversight. You use it to download torrents, visit sketchy sites, and click every "Your Flash Player is Outdated" ad that appears.
Connecting that device to the corporate VPN is like inviting a stranger with a contagious disease into a hospital ward.
"But I needed to check my email quickly" â€” install the company-approved email app on your phone. Do not bridge your cesspool of a personal laptop into the corporate network.
Note: The VPN is a privileged access tunnel. Treat it like one. Do not let unsecured devices through the front door.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU LOG INTO THE VPN FROM A COMPROMISED PERSONAL DEVICE...

bullets: "Can you just make it faster?" is the most technically illiterate question in IT. It assumes there is a "speed slider" somewhere in the settings that I have been hiding from you.
I cannot make your 5-year-old laptop with a spinning hard drive run like a new M-series Mac. The laws of physics have already set the maximum speed of your hardware.
"Can you just upgrade my RAM?" â€” that is not a "just." That is a hardware intervention. It costs money and takes time. Also, your laptop's RAM is soldered. So no.
Note: "Make it faster" is not a request. It is a wish. I am a technician, not a genie.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST MAKE IT FASTER?'...

bullets: Admin rights allow you to install any software, modify any system file, and completely destroy the OS in ways that require a full reimage to fix.
"I need admin rights to install a PDF reader" â€” no, you do not. The company-approved PDF reader is already in the software centre. Click install. No admin rights required.
"I will be careful" â€” everyone says that. Then they install a toolbar, a "free" screensaver, and a driver updater from a pop-up ad. Then they call me to fix the mess.
Note: Admin rights are not a privilege. They are a liability waiver. Every admin user is one bad click away from a reimage.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST GIVE ME ADMIN RIGHTS?'...

bullets: Your colleague has a specific set of software, permissions, and configurations that were set up over months of troubleshooting. I cannot "just copy" a human's workflow.
"We do the same job, why can't I have what they have?" â€” because you have different requirements, different access needs, and different software licenses.
Also, your colleague's machine is a mess. They have 47 browser extensions, 3 expired antivirus trials, and a desktop cluttered with files named "final_v3_REAL(1).docx." You do not want their setup.
Note: "Copy their setup" is not a technical request. It is a complaint about fairness dressed up as an IT issue.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST COPY MY COLLEAGUE'S SETUP?'...

bullets: The website is blocked by the firewall because it is classified as "gambling," "adult content," or "malware distribution." There is a reason it is blocked.
"I need it for research" â€” you do not. You want to access it on company time. The firewall logs will confirm which category it falls under.
Requesting an unblock requires manager approval. Your manager will be notified of the request. If the site is work-related, they will approve it. If it is not, they will not.
Note: "Can you just unblock this?" is a request for me to bypass security policy. I will not. Ask your manager to submit the formal request.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST UNLOCK THIS WEBSITE?'...

bullets: "A quick look" is never quick. It is a 45-minute investigation that starts with "I will just check one thing" and ends with me rebuilding your Outlook profile, resetting your browser, and updating 14 drivers.
"A quick look" is how unpaid overtime is born. It is how a 5-minute fix becomes a 2-hour pro-bono support session.
If it needs looking at, submit a ticket. If it is urgent, call. If it is neither, wait. "A quick look" is not a valid support channel.
Note: "Can you just look?" is the precursor to "While you are here..." which is the precursor to me regretting my life choices.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST TAKE A QUICK LOOK?'...

bullets: I cannot see your screen over the phone. I cannot click buttons for you over the phone. I cannot run diagnostics over the phone.
"I will describe what is happening" â€” your description will be "there is an error." That is not a description. That is a state of being.
Remote support requires a remote connection or a ticket with detailed information. Pick one. "Just fix it" is not actionable.
Note: IT support over the phone is limited to "turn it off and on again." If you need more than that, I need access to your machine.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST FIX IT OVER THE PHONE?'...

bullets: An exception for you means an exception for everyone. Once I bend the rule for one person, I cannot enforce it for anyone else.
"Just this once" â€” and next week you will ask again. And the week after that. And then everyone in your department will ask for the same exception.
Security policies exist because of the aggregate behaviour of everyone before you who asked for "just one exception" and then caused a breach.
Note: "Just one exception" is how security policies die. The answer is no. It will always be no.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST MAKE AN EXCEPTION?'...

bullets: If the request starts with "Can you just," it is probably more complicated than you think.
If it were a "just," you would have done it yourself.
"Just" is the most dangerous word in IT support. It minimises the effort, trivialises the complexity, and guarantees the requester has no idea what they are asking for.
Note: Remove "just" from your vocabulary when talking to IT. Say what you need, let me decide how complicated it is.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK 'CAN YOU JUST...' ANYTHING...

bullets: I manage servers, networks, and software deployments. I do not manage pneumatic gas cylinders, castor wheels, or lumbar support adjustments.
"The chair won't stay up" â€” that is a gas lift mechanism. It is mechanical, not digital. I cannot reboot your chair.
"It makes a clicking noise when I lean back" â€” stop leaning back at a 45-degree angle with your feet on the desk. Chairs are not rocking horses.
Note: IT stands for Information Technology, not Interior Technology. Call facilities or procurement. Leave us out of your ergonomic crisis.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BLAME IT FOR YOUR BROKEN OFFICE CHAIR...

bullets: Chairs do not "just break." They break because you weigh 120kg and you sit on the edge of the cushion with all your weight on the front rim, or you spin violently in it like a carnival ride.
The same person who breaks a chair every 6 months and blames "poor quality" is not unlucky. They are a repeating pattern with a common variable.
"It was fine yesterday" â€” and a car with worn brake pads was "fine yesterday" until it was not. Wear and tear is a thing. You are not the victim of a chair conspiracy.
Note: If you have broken 4 chairs in 3 years, the problem is not the chairs. The problem is how you interact with chairs.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLAIM YOUR CHAIR 'JUST BROKE'...

bullets: The armrest is held on by bolts. Bolts require a hex key, not a software patch. I do not carry a hex key. I carry a screwdriver for opening server chassis.
"Can you just order me a new chair?" â€” I can order you a new docking station. I cannot order you a new throne. Submit a procurement request.
The chair is not a peripheral device. It does not connect via USB. It does not need drivers. It is a chair. Sit in it properly and it will last.
Note: Our support contract covers laptops, monitors, and docking stations. It does not cover the thing you sit on while using them.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK IT TO FIX THE CHAIR ARMEST...

bullets: The chair is not stuck. You spun it 15 times in one direction for fun and now the tension in the gas cylinder is twisted. Untwist it by spinning the other way the same number of times.
Office chairs are not amusement park rides. They are ergonomic tools. Treat them with the respect they do not deserve.
"It is leaning to one side" â€” because you sit with your legs crossed and all your weight on one hip every single day for 8 hours. The foam has memory. It remembers your bad posture.
Note: A chair that leans to one side is not broken. It is a mirror reflecting your asymmetrical sitting habits.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SPIN IN YOUR CHAIR AND CLAIM IT IS 'STUCK'...

bullets: Let me guess: `Report.docx`, `Report_v2.docx`, `Report_v3.docx`, `Report_FINAL.docx`, `Report_FINAL_REAL.docx`, `Report_FINAL_REAL_2.docx`, `Report_FINAL_REAL_3_USE_THIS.docx`, `Report_FINAL_REAL_3_USE_THIS_OMG.docx`, `Report_ACTUALLY_FINAL.docx`
Every single one of these is a different version of the same document, all in the same folder, with no indication of what changed between them.
Version control software exists. Git exists. Even "Save As" with a date stamp would be an improvement over whatever this chaos is.
Note: A folder with 47 files all named "final" with slight variations is not a filing system. It is a cry for help.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAVE THE SAME FILE 17 TIMES WITH DIFFERENT NAMES...

bullets: You saved a new document, and instead of giving it a descriptive name, you pressed Enter on the default "Document1" and closed it forever.
In three weeks, you will need that file. You will search for it. "Document1" will not help you. There are 14 files named "Document1" on your drive.
The 10 seconds it takes to type a meaningful filename now will save you 30 minutes of frantic searching later. This is not complicated.
Note: "Document1" is not a filename. It is a placeholder that you accepted as permanent. Name your files like an adult.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU NAME A FILE 'Document1.docx'...

bullets: `2024-01-15.docx`, `2024-02-03.docx`, `2024-03-22.docx` â€” great, you know when you created them. But what ARE they? Meeting minutes? A report? A grocery list?
Dates are useful AS PART of a filename, not as the ENTIRE filename. Combine the date with a descriptive title. This is not an either/or situation.
"I will know what it is by the date" â€” you will not. Future you will curse past you for this arrogance.
Note: A filename that only contains a date is a timestamp, not a label. You are not an archive system.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE ONLY DATES TO NAME FILES...

bullets: Your desktop has 147 files on it. They fill the entire screen. The wallpaper is completely obscured. You cannot see the recycle bin. This is not "easy access." This is digital hoarding.
"I know where everything is" â€” you do not. You scroll for 30 seconds every time you need a file. You squint at tiny icons and read truncated filenames. This is not efficiency. It is denial.
The desktop is not a filing cabinet. It is a temporary workspace. Files belong in folders. Folders belong in directories. Directories belong on drives. This hierarchy exists for a reason.
Note: A desktop cluttered with files is not a badge of productivity. It is a symptom of disorganisation.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAVE FILES TO THE DESKTOP 'FOR EASY ACCESS'...

bullets: `REPORT_FINAL_REALLY_IMPORTANT_DO_NOT_DELETE_V2.DOCX` â€” I can see it is important. I can also see you have no restraint.
All caps in filenames is the digital equivalent of shouting. The file is not shouting. You are shouting on behalf of the file.
Also, YOU_CANNOT_PUT_SPACES_IN_FILENAMES_LIKE_THIS_EITHER. Underscores are not spaces. They are underscores. They do not make the filename better.
Note: A filename should describe the content, not your emotional state about the content. Lowercase is allowed. Use it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE ALL CAPS IN FILENAMES...

bullets: The recycle bin is not a storage location. It is a holding cell for files awaiting deletion. Files in the recycle bin are one "Empty Recycle Bin" click away from oblivion.
"I keep my important files there so I can restore them if I delete them by accident" â€” that is not how any of this works. That is like parking your car in a crusher "just in case."
The recycle bin is emptied automatically on a schedule. Your "important" files are being routinely purged by a process that does not know they are special.
Note: Storing files in the recycle bin is not a backup strategy. It is a ticking time bomb. Move your files to a real folder.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU STORE CRITICAL FILES ONLY IN THE RECYCLE BIN...

bullets: Standing directly behind a colleague and breathing down their neck while they troubleshoot does not make the computer work faster. It makes the person work slower.
"Is it fixed yet?" asked every 45 seconds for 15 minutes does not constitute technical support. It constitutes psychological warfare.
The machine does not respond to audience pressure. It does not perform better under observation. Your presence is not helping.
Note: Watching someone type is not a team sport. Go back to your desk. We will call you when it is done.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU STAND BEHIND SOMEONE WHILE THEY WORK...

bullets: "Quickly" is the longest unit of time in IT support. It starts as 30 seconds and expands to fill the entire afternoon.
You have walked across the office, interrupted someone mid-task, and now expect them to drop everything because you did not submit a ticket.
The issue you are about to describe has been happening for 3 weeks. It is not urgent. You just decided now is the time to deal with it â€” which happens to be when the technician is busy.
Note: A physical ambush at someone's desk is not a support channel. Submit a ticket like a civilised person.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BRING YOUR LAPTOP TO SOMEONE'S DESK AND SAY 'JUST LOOK AT THIS QUICKLY'...

bullets: I have a name. It is on my email signature. It is on my office door. It is on the company directory. Use it.
Shouting "Hey IT!" across an open-plan office while 30 people turn around to see who is summoning me like a summoned demon is disrespectful to everyone involved.
"Hey, while you are here..." â€” I am not "here." I was walking to the bathroom. I was going home. I was in the middle of something. You do not get to hijack my trajectory.
Note: If you see me in the hallway, the cafeteria, or the parking lot, that is not an invitation to open a support ticket.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL OUT 'HEY IT GUY!' FROM ACROSS THE ROOM...

bullets: The IT room door is closed because I am concentrating on something that requires focus. Knocking every 30 seconds does not make me finish faster.
"I know the door is closed but this is quick" â€” the door is closed. That is a sign. It means "do not disturb." It does not mean "knock until someone answers."
The number of times you knock is inversely proportional to how helpful I will be when I finally open the door.
Note: A closed door means "I am busy." A locked door means "I am very busy and I do not trust you." A door with a sign that says "Do Not Disturb" means I have already guessed you would ignore it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU KNOCK ON THE IT ROOM DOOR REPEATEDLY...

bullets: Reading my screen over my shoulder is not collaboration. It is surveillance. I do not come to your desk and read your email over your shoulder.
"I am just interested in what you are doing" â€” I am terminating a process. It looks exactly like a black screen with white text. There is nothing interesting here. Go away.
Every time I sense someone watching my screen, I make an error. That error costs time. That time is billable to your department.
Note: The window into my soul is behind my eyes, not on my monitor. Personal space applies to screens too.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU WATCH OVER MY SHOULDER WHILE I WORK...

bullets: You just changed your password 30 seconds ago. You wrote it on a sticky note. You stuck the sticky note to your monitor. You then closed the change-password window and immediately forgot what you typed.
"I do not remember my new password" â€” you set it. You confirmed it. You watched the confirmation message. The password is somewhere between your short-term and long-term memory, lost in transit.
This is the third time this month. The password policy has not changed. The process has not changed. Your approach to remembering things has not changed either, apparently.
Note: A password reset that you forget within 60 seconds is not a technical issue. It is a cognitive one. Write it down somewhere that is not your hand.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU RESET YOUR PASSWORD AND FORGET IT IMMEDIATELY...

bullets: You did not need to reset your password. Your password was not compromised. The system did not prompt you to reset it. You "just felt like it" and now you cannot log in.
Every reset increases the chance that you will lock yourself out, forget the new password, or write it down somewhere insecure.
"I thought it was a good idea" â€” it was not. The password was working fine. You fixed something that was not broken, and now you have broken it.
Note: Proactive password changes without being prompted are not security best practice. They are self-inflicted wounds.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU RESET YOUR PASSWORD AGAIN 'JUST TO BE SAFE'...

bullets: `Password1` â†’ `Password2` â†’ `Password3` does not fool anyone. The system remembers. The password history check exists specifically to catch this.
"I just add a number at the end" â€” yes. Everyone does. That is why password history checks look for exactly that pattern.
If I can guess your new password based on your last 5 passwords, so can an attacker with a basic script.
Note: Rotating through `Spring2024`, `Summer2024`, `Autumn2024` is not password security. It is a calendar with letters.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE THE SAME PASSWORD WITH ONE CHARACTER CHANGED...

bullets: Your account is locked because you entered the wrong password too many times. It is locked because you kept guessing. You guessed wrong 5 times in a row.
"I am sure it is the right password" â€” it is not. The system is sure it is not. The system is never wrong about this. You are.
At some point, the definition of insanity doing the same thing and expecting different results applies directly to your password entry behaviour.
Note: We have a self-service unlock portal. It sends a code to your phone. If you cannot remember your password and cannot use the portal, we have reached a new level of helplessness.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT TO UNLOCK YOUR ACCOUNT FOR THE 5TH TIME THIS MONTH...

bullets: Caps Lock is on. It is always on. I have never encountered a user who checked Caps Lock before calling IT.
You are typing your password into the "Username" field. The system is rejecting it because "Administrator" is not a valid password. That is correct behaviour.
You changed your password 5 minutes ago and are now trying to log in with your old password. The old password was replaced. It does not work anymore.
Note: 90% of "my password does not work" calls are solved by turning off Caps Lock. 90% of the remaining 10% are solved by reading the screen. Read the screen before calling.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK WHY YOUR NEW PASSWORD 'IS NOT WORKING'...

bullets: A sticky note on your monitor is visible to everyone who walks past your desk, including the cleaning staff, visitors, and the person who will later use it to send emails from your account.
"I trust everyone in the office" â€” security is not about trust. It is about preventing the one person who should not have access from having access.
If you need to write your password down, use a password manager. If you refuse to use a password manager, at least put the sticky note inside your drawer, not on your screen.
Note: A password on a sticky note stuck to the monitor is not a "system." It is a "security incident waiting to happen."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU WRITE YOUR PASSWORD ON A STICKY NOTE...

bullets: You just printed 200 full-colour pages, walked to the printer, grabbed the single page you actually needed, and left the remaining 199 pages in the tray. This is not an accident. You do this every time.
The remaining pages sit in the output tray until someone else either throws them away, adds them to the growing pile of orphaned print jobs, or takes them home by mistake.
Every page you abandon costs the company money. Toner is not cheap. Paper is not free. The environment is not a fan of your habits either.
Note: The print queue is not a "selective harvesting system." If you print it, take it. All of it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PRINT 200 PAGES AND TAKE ONLY 1...

bullets: That internal memo did not need to be printed in colour. The spreadsheet did not need colour. The 50-page training manual definitely did not need colour.
Colour toner costs 5 times more than black toner. Printing 200 pages of internal documentation in full colour is not "making it look nice." It is burning the office supply budget.
"But the charts have different coloured lines" â€” the lines are labelled. The legend exists. Black and white is sufficient. You are not designing a brochure.
Note: Colour printing is for client-facing materials and approved marketing collateral. Your Monday morning status report does not qualify.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PRINT IN COLOUR 'BECAUSE IT LOOKS NICER'...

bullets: Printing a 300-page PDF, a 150-page research report, and an entire website "to read later" â€” you will not read it later. You will leave it on the printer until someone throws it away.
"I like to have a hard copy" â€” then print it, bind it, and file it. Do not print it and let it accumulate in a pile on top of the printer that nobody touches for 6 months.
The printer is not a publishing house. It is a utilitarian device for occasional document production, not a Gutenberg press for your digital hoarding.
Note: Paperless was supposed to reduce printing. You interpreted it as a challenge to print more before it is too late.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PRINT THE ENTIRE INTERNET 'JUST IN CASE'...

bullets: The printer is chugging through a 50-page document. You pressed Print, turned around, and walked back to your desk. You will return in 20 minutes and the pages will have been taken by someone else.
"I will come back in a few minutes" â€” those few minutes turn into an hour, then the next day, then never. Your orphaned print job becomes a permanent resident of the output tray.
Corporate printers are not restaurant kitchens. They do not call out your order number when it is ready. Stand there for 47 seconds and collect your pages.
Note: The walk of shame back to an empty printer tray with no pages and a growing pile of someone else's abandoned documents is self-inflicted.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU WALK AWAY FROM THE PRINTER WHILE IT IS STILL PRINTING...

bullets: The paper tray has a diagram. The diagram shows which way the paper faces, which side is up, and how to align the edges. You ignored the diagram and now the paper is jammed at a 30-degree angle.
There is a label inside the tray that says "This side up." You put it "this side down." The printer does not know which way is up. It just tries to feed what you gave it.
You loaded 15 sheets of paper loosely on top of a half-empty ream and expected the feeder to handle the height difference gracefully. It did not.
Note: Paper loading is not a guessing game. Follow the diagram. The diagram exists because someone before you failed at this exact task.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU LOAD PAPER INCORRECTLY AND BLAME THE PRINTER...

bullets: Is the printer on? Check the power light. Do not call me before checking the power light.
Is there paper in the tray? Look at the tray. Open it. Check. Do not call me before checking the paper tray.
Is the toner empty? The printer will tell you on its screen. Look at the screen. Read the message. Do not call me before reading the message on the screen.
Note: The printer has an LCD display. It shows error messages. Read the error message before calling IT. The message "Paper Jam" means there is a paper jam. It does not mean "call IT immediately."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CALL IT BECAUSE THE PRINTER 'IS NOT PRINTING'...

bullets: You invited 14 people to a 1-hour meeting to read a spreadsheet out loud. The spreadsheet was sent as an attachment in the invitation. Everyone could have read it in 5 minutes at their desk.
14 people Ã— 60 minutes = 14 person-hours spent on something that could have been accomplished with a 5-minute email. That is 13 hours and 55 minutes of collective life wasted.
"I wanted to discuss it" â€” discuss what? The numbers are on the page. The trends are visible. The decisions can be made via email. You called a meeting because you did not want to write an email.
Note: A meeting where one person talks and everyone else listens is called a "presentation." Those can be recorded and watched at 1.5x speed. Do not book my calendar for a monologue.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SCHEDULE A 1-HOUR MEETING TO READ A SPREADSHEET...

bullets: A status update for the 3-person project team does not need to include the CEO, the board, the entire marketing department, and that intern from accounting who has never heard of this project.
"Just in case they are interested" â€” if they are interested, they will read the meeting notes. You do not need to occupy their calendar for an hour to keep them "in the loop."
Every person in that room is billing their time to a department. Your meeting is costing the company thousands of rands per hour. For a status update that could have been a bullet-point list.
Note: "Covering all bases" is not a justification for calendar terrorism.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU INVITE THE ENTIRE COMPANY TO A STATUS UPDATE...

bullets: A meeting invitation with no agenda, no context, and a title like "Quick catch-up" is a black hole of productivity. Nobody knows what to prepare, what to bring, or why they are there.

"We will figure it out when we get there" â€” no. We will spend the first 15 minutes figuring out what the meeting is about, then rush through the actual content, then schedule a follow-up because we ran out of time.
An agenda is not optional. It is the minimum viable requirement for any meeting. If you cannot write 3 bullet points about what the meeting covers, you are not ready to hold it.
Note: A meeting without an agenda is a social gathering. Schedule it after hours if you want to socialise.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BOOK A MEETING WITHOUT AN AGENDA...

bullets: There are 18 people in this meeting. You work in the same company. Some of you sit 3 desks apart. You do not need introductions. You need to respect everyone's time.
"I want everyone to feel included" â€” everyone will feel included when the meeting ends on time and they can get back to work. Not when they have to listen to 18 people recite their job titles.
If you do not know who is in the room, check the calendar invitation. You sent it. You should know who you invited.
Note: Round-robin introductions in a meeting of more than 6 people is a hostage situation, not team building.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU START THE MEETING WITH 'LET'S GO AROUND THE ROOM AND INTRODUCE OURSELVES'...

bullets: The first meeting ran over because there was no agenda, no timekeeping, and no decision-making. The follow-up will run over for the same reasons.
You are not solving the problem by booking more time. You are compounding the problem by doubling the wasted time.
If the first meeting did not achieve its objective, the solution is not a second meeting. The solution is a clear agenda, pre-reading materials, and a strict time limit for the first meeting.
Note: A follow-up meeting to "continue the discussion" is an admission that the first meeting was a failure. Fix the process, not the calendar.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BOOK A FOLLOW-UP MEETING BECAUSE THE FIRST ONE RAN OVER...

bullets: "Let's sync up" is the vaguest meeting title in corporate history. It communicates nothing about the purpose, the expected outcome, or what attendees need to prepare.
Sync up on what? The project status? The roadmap? The coffee machine maintenance schedule? I cannot prepare for a meeting if I do not know what it is about.
"Sync" implies two-way communication. If you are going to talk at me for 45 minutes with 5 minutes for questions, that is not a sync. That is a broadcast.
Note: "Sync up" is the corporate equivalent of "we need to talk." It fills everyone with dread and accomplishes nothing.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BOOK A MEETING FOR 'SYNCING UP'...

bullets: The meeting could have been an email. Now it is a recorded meeting that nobody will watch because it is 60 minutes long and could have been summarised in 3 bullet points.
"I will send the recording afterwards" â€” you will not. But even if you do, nobody will watch it. They will skim the transcript if one exists, or they will ask you in Slack what was decided.
The recording is not a substitute for proper documentation. Write down the decisions, action items, and next steps. That is what people need, not a video of 14 people staring at a spreadsheet.
Note: A recorded meeting is not documentation. It is digital archaeology. Future generations will not excavate your Teams recording to find out why the budget was approved.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU RECORD THE MEETING 'FOR THOSE WHO COULD NOT ATTEND'...

title: The Meeting That Could Have Been an Email
description: The Meeting That Could Have Been an Email

bullets: You found a USB stick in the parking lot and your first instinct was to plug it into the work PC. That is not curiosity. That is a digital suicide wish.
The USB stick from the conference swag bag went straight into your laptop without a second thought. You do not know who handled that stick before you. You do not know what else is on it.
"It was in my drawer for three years, it's probably fine." Three years is not a sterilization period. Malware does not have an expiration date.
The "I found it in the break room" defense does not hold up when the entire network goes down.
You picked up a USB stick from the parking lot and plugged it in because you thought it might contain "interesting files." It did contain files. They were encrypting your hard drive.
You found a USB stick labeled "Salary Data 2025" and plugged it in immediately. It was not salary data. It was a keystroke logger.
The USB stick was shaped like a rubber duck. That is not cute. That is a Rubber Ducky attack. It is typing commands as fast as the human thumb can manage â€” except it is not a human thumb.
You saw a USB stick on the floor and thought "free storage." It was free storage the same way a bear trap is free footwear.
The colleague who said "I ran a virus scan on it" ran Windows Defender once in 2019. That scan result is not valid.
You collected USB sticks from the lost-and-found bin and tested each one "just to see." You saw the inside of a ransomware screen.
"I only opened one file." That is how it starts. Patient zero never says "I opened all of them."
You tried to charge your phone using a USB port on a public kiosk. That is called juice jacking. Your phone is now exfiltrating data to a stranger.
The USB stick was left on your desk with a note that said "urgent." Urgent is a red flag. Real urgent documents are sent via email with a proper chain of custody.
You bought a cheap USB hub from a random vendor at a tech flea market. The hub contains a hidden chip that logs every keystroke you make through it.
The USB stick came free with a subscription box. Free hardware is never free. The cost is your network integrity.
You plugged in a USB stick from a vendor at a trade show without asking IT to vet it first. That vendor's logo does not make it safe.
"I formatted it first." Formatting does not fix hardware-level exploits. The controller chip can be reprogrammed to inject malware on format.
You found a microSD card on the sidewalk and used it in your dashcam. That microSD now has remote access to your home network.
The USB stick was given to you by a user who said "it has a virus, can you fix it?" and you plugged it into your machine instead of an isolated sandbox.
You still have the USB stick from your previous company and you plugged it into your new work computer. That is how cross-contamination works in the digital world.
You thought BadUSB was a myth. It is not a myth. It is a proven attack vector and you just inserted patient zero into the company network.
You plugged a USB stick into the server because "it needed a driver." Servers do not need drivers from unidentified USB sticks. Servers need isolation.
The USB stick was attached to a keychain that also had a company badge. That badge now looks like an endorsement. It is not.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PLUG THAT MYSTERY USB STICK INTO YOUR WORK COMPUTER...

bullets: You tried to fix it yourself. Now it is not only still broken, but it is also broken in a way that is harder to diagnose because I now have to undo whatever you did before I can even see the original problem.
"I ran a registry cleaner" â€” you did not fix the issue. You deleted 400 critical system entries. The original problem is still there, now compounded by a lobotomised OS.

"I uninstalled some programs I did not recognise" â€” you uninstalled the VPN client, the antivirus, and the print driver. The original issue was that your email signature was wrong. You have now created 3 new problems.
Note: "I tried to fix it" is the most expensive preface in IT support. The diagnostic fee doubles when I have to reverse your 'help.'
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU 'FIX' THE PROBLEM BEFORE CALLING IT...

bullets: The YouTube video is called "How to Speed Up Windows 10." The steps include disabling services, deleting prefetch files, and modifying the registry. None of these apply to your specific issue.
The video was made by a 19-year-old in his bedroom who has never managed a corporate network. His advice is not applicable to your enterprise environment.
You followed the steps exactly. The steps were wrong. Your machine is now slower, less secure, and 3 critical services have been disabled. Congratulations.
Note: YouTube is not a certification. A tutorial from a stranger is not IT support. Close the video and call the helpdesk.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU WATCH A YOUTUBE VIDEO AND FOLLOW THE STEPS...

bullets: Your friend knows how to build a gaming PC. That does not mean they know how to configure a corporate VPN, troubleshoot a print server, or recover a corrupted Outlook profile.
"He fixed it before" â€” he fixed it by reinstalling Windows. That is not "fixing." That is the nuclear option. He did not solve the problem. He nuked it from orbit and hoped it would not come back.

Now your friend has uninstalled the company antivirus and installed a "lighter" one he found online. Your machine is no longer compliant with our security policy and will be quarantined from the network.
Note: Your friend's "fix" just created a compliance violation. We now have to reimage your machine entirely. Thanks for the help.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK YOUR 'TECH SAVVY' FRIEND TO 'TAKE A LOOK'...

bullets: The browser was slow because you had 47 extensions installed and 200 tabs open. Reinstalling the operating system fixes that, but at what cost? You just wiped every file, setting, and configuration that was not backed up.

"I backed up my files first" â€” you backed up your Documents folder. You did not back up your Outlook signature, your saved Wi-Fi passwords, your browser bookmarks, or the configuration files for the 6 line-of-business applications you use daily.
A slow browser is not an operating system problem. It is a "clean your browser" problem. You escalated this from a 5-minute fix to a 4-hour rebuild.
Note: Reinstalling Windows because Chrome is slow is like demolishing your house because the sink is clogged.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REINSTALL WINDOWS 'TO FIX A SLOW BROWSER'...

bullets: The first result on Google is a forum post from 2012 where someone suggested deleting a DLL file. That DLL file is used by 3 critical applications. You deleted it. Those applications no longer work.

"The forum post said it worked for them" â€” it worked for them on their specific configuration, with their specific OS version, and their specific hardware. Yours is different. The result is different.
Googling error messages is what IT does. The difference is we know which results are relevant, which are outdated, and which will destroy your machine. You do not have that filter.
Note: Dr. Google is not a licensed IT practitioner. WebMD for computers has the same reliability as WebMD for humans: terrifying and usually wrong.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU 'GOOGLE THE ERROR MESSAGE' AND FOLLOW THE FIRST RESULT...

bullets: You submitted a ticket asking for a password reset and CC'd the CEO. The CEO does not care about your forgotten password. The CEO now has an email about your forgotten password. This is not the impression you think it is.
CC'ing executives on routine IT issues does not make the issue resolve faster. It makes the IT team resent you and the executives question your competence.

"I wanted to make sure it was taken seriously" â€” all tickets are taken seriously. Your attempt to bypass the queue by invoking executive authority has just landed your ticket in a special queue. The "reviewed by legal" queue.
Note: CC'ing the CEO on a password reset ticket is the IT equivalent of calling the fire department because your toast is burnt.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CC THE CEO ON A TIER 1 SUPPORT TICKET...

bullets: Your font is not printing correctly. That is not urgent. Urgent is "the server is on fire." Urgent is "the entire billing system is offline." Urgent is not "Word is showing the wrong margins."

When every ticket is marked urgent, urgent loses all meaning. Your false urgency means that when there is an actual emergency, genuine urgent tickets get lost in the noise of your "my desktop wallpaper changed" false alarms.
The system tracks how many of your tickets are actually urgent. The ratio is not in your favour. The data does not lie.
Note: If everything is urgent, nothing is urgent. Your font issue will be handled in the order it was received, which is after the server fire.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE 'URGENT' ON A NON-URGENT TICKET...

bullets: "Board-level priority" is a phrase people use when they want their routine request fast-tracked. The board has never heard of you or your spreadsheet formatting issue.
If the board is genuinely involved, I will know about it before you do. The board does not send intermediaries. The board calls directly.
Invoking the board's name does not grant you executive privilege. It grants you a special flag on your account that reads "User claims board involvement. Usually untrue."
Note: The board is not your personal IT escalation hotline. Do not use their name in vain.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'THIS IS A BOARD-LEVEL PRIORITY'...

bullets: Emailing 10 different IT staff members the same request does not create 10 parallel work streams. It creates 10 people who are all confused about who is handling it, resulting in either duplicate work or everyone assuming someone else will handle it.

"I wanted to make sure someone saw it" â€” all 10 people saw it. None of them are responding because they are waiting for the other 9 to take ownership. You have effectively paralysed the entire support team.
The support queue is a single, organised system. Sending emails to individual staff members bypasses that system and guarantees your request will be handled slower, not faster.
Note: Spray-and-pray emailing to the entire IT department is not escalation. It is noise generation. Pick one person and wait.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SEND A TICKET TO 10 DIFFERENT PEOPLE AT ONCE...

bullets: If you needed it yesterday, you should have submitted it yesterday. The fact that you submitted it 5 minutes ago and are demanding yesterday-level turnaround is not a scheduling conflict on my end. It is a planning failure on yours.
"I know it is last minute, but..." â€” if you know it is last minute, you had time to anticipate it. You chose not to. Your lack of planning does not constitute my emergency.
Time machines do not exist in our software stack. I cannot backdate my work. I can only work forward from the moment you actually submitted the request.
Note: A "needed by yesterday" deadline submitted today is called "a failure to plan." The IT department does not have a time machine.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'I NEED THIS BY YESTERDAY'...

bullets: Your mouse battery is low. You added the IT Director to the ticket. The IT Director does not change mouse batteries. The IT Director manages the team that changes mouse batteries. You have now escalated a battery replacement to executive leadership.
Adding senior leadership to a low-level ticket does not make it more important. It makes you look like you cannot handle a mouse battery replacement without involving the chain of command.
The IT Director's daily rate is approximately R12,000. They just spent 30 seconds reading your mouse battery ticket. That cost the company R83 of executive time for a problem that costs R5 to fix.
Note: Low-level tickets with executive CCs are not impressive. They are embarrassing for everyone involved.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ADD THE IT DIRECTOR TO A TICKET ABOUT A MINOR ISSUE...

bullets: The email was sent to 500 people. It says "For your information" in the subject line. It does not require a response. It certainly does not require a response sent to 500 people.
You clicked Reply-All to say "Thanks, noted." 500 people now have an email in their inbox that says "Thanks, noted." None of them wanted this. None of them care.
The 47 subsequent "Please remove me from this thread" replies are your fault. You started the avalanche. You are the reason reply-all disasters happen.
Note: Reply-All is not a greeting card delivery system. "Thanks" sent to 500 colleagues is not polite. It is spam.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REPLY-ALL TO A COMPANY-WIDE EMAIL...

bullets: It is an email chain about the quarterly financial results. Someone accidentally included the entire company. Your response asking about the birthday cake is now visible to 500 people, including the CEO and the board.
The reply-all cake question will become a legendary story that is told in this company for years. You will be the punchline. Your name will be synonymous with the Great Cake Incident.
There is a reason email etiquette training exists. This is the reason. You are the cautionary tale they will use.
Note: The cake comment should have been a direct reply. You have now been permanently labelled "the cake person" in the IT department's internal chat.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REPLY-ALL WITH 'WHO IS BRINGING THE CAKE?'...

bullets: You are receiving a company-wide email because you work here. You cannot "unsubscribe" from the company newsletter by replying to it. That is not how distribution lists work.
Replying "Please remove me from this list" to 500 people does not remove you from the list. It proves to 500 people that you do not understand how email works.
The only person who can remove you from the list is the list administrator. That person is not on the reply-all. Email your manager, not the entire company.
Note: Reply-All is not an unsubscribe button. It is a megaphone. You just broadcasted your ignorance to the entire organisation.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU HIT REPLY-ALL TO UNSUBSCRIBE...

bullets: You forwarded a chain email that says "Send this to 10 people or you will have bad luck for 7 years" to the entire company directory. This is not a cultural tradition. This is a workplace hazard.
The chain email was already debunked in 2005. It contains 47 previous forward headers, a rainbow of font colours, and a clip art image of a kitten. This is not professional communication.
Forwarding chain emails at work is grounds for a mandatory email etiquette training session. You have volunteered yourself as the primary example.
Note: Chain emails in a corporate environment are not "sharing." They are "polluting the professional communication channel with digital superstition."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU FORWARD A CHAIN EMAIL TO THE COMPANY...

bullets: You set an out-of-office auto-reply. Someone sent a company-wide email. Your out-of-office auto-replied to all 500 recipients. 500 people now know you are on leave. None of them needed to know.
Out-of-office replies should go to the sender only, not the entire distribution list. Most email systems handle this correctly. Yours apparently did not. Or you configured it incorrectly.
A company-wide email thread now has 23 out-of-office replies interspersed with the original content. The thread is useless. The noise has consumed the signal.
Note: An out-of-office reply sent to 500 people is not a vacation notification. It is a broadcast of your inability to configure email settings.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REPLY-ALL WITH YOUR OUT OF OFFICE...

bullets: Again. This is the second book in the Bible about this exact sin. It is so common it needs two chapters.
Yes, the IT department sent a fake "You have a package" email. Yes, you not only clicked the link, but you also replied-all asking "Did anyone else get this?" to 500 people.
The phishing test was designed to catch one person. You have now identified yourself to 500 people as the one who failed. HR has been notified. Training has been assigned.
Note: Reply-All on a phishing test is the seventh circle of email hell. Dante did not write about it because he could not have imagined this level of self-exposure.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU REPLY-ALL TO A PHISHING TEST...

bullets: You have been postponing the same Windows Update for 6 months. The "Remind me later" button is tired. The system is tired. I am tired. The update is not going away.

Every update you postpone is a security patch you are not applying. Those patches fix vulnerabilities that are being actively exploited in the wild. Your procrastination is a security risk to the entire network.
"It worked fine before the update" is not an argument. It worked fine before the update because previous updates kept it working fine. The update you are declining is the reason it kept working fine.
You turned off automatic updates because they were "annoying." You know what is more annoying? Ransomware encrypting every file on the server.
You said "I don't trust Microsoft updates." You are running Windows on a Microsoft network. That ship has sailed. You already trust them with your data. Trust them with the patches.
The blue screen you got after an update three years ago is not justification for declining every update forever.
You are still on Windows 10 because you "heard Windows 11 has bugs." Windows 10 is approaching end of life. No more security patches.
You postponed a critical security update 47 times. The notification badge is showing a 4 and a 7. That is not a count. That is an indictment.
You think restarting for updates takes too long. The ransomware recovery will take much longer.
Your phone has 37 pending OS updates. Every unpatched vulnerability on your phone is a backdoor into the network.
You declined a firmware update because "it might break something." Firmware updates patch hardware-level vulnerabilities. The thing that will break is your security posture.
You are running an unsupported operating system because you "prefer the interface." The interface does not matter when there are no security patches.
You set your network connection to "metered" specifically to block Windows Update from downloading. That is not clever. That is sabotage.
You use third-party software to disable updates entirely. That software does not disable vulnerabilities. It disables protection.
The update failed once, so you hid it permanently. Update failures can be fixed. Zero-day exploits cannot.
You uninstalled a security update because it "slowed down Excel." A slightly slower spreadsheet is better than a compromised network.
You do not believe in patches. Patches are not a belief system. They fix holes that exist whether you believe in them or not.
You restart your computer once a year whether it needs it or not. It needs it. Monthly is the minimum. Weekly is better.
You are using software from 2018 because "the new version has a different layout." Using unsupported software is a security vulnerability.
You pay for extended support on an outdated OS because you refuse to upgrade. That is paying rent on a sinking ship.
You turned off your antivirus because it was "using too much CPU." The malware using 100% CPU is going to be a lot less convenient.
The VPN update notification has been sitting there for two months. An unpatched VPN client is an open door to the corporate network.
You do not update your browser because you "like the old tab design." The old design does not include the latest security sandboxing.
You clicked "don't show this again" on a critical update notification. The notification is gone. The vulnerability is not.
You think IT sends updates to annoy you personally. We do not have the time or the inclination to personally annoy every user.
You declined a BIOS update. The BIOS is the first thing that runs when you press the power button. Compromised BIOS means compromised everything.
You use the motto "if it ain't broke, don't fix it." Security is not a repair strategy. It is a maintenance strategy. Update before the breach.
Your printer has a pending firmware update from 2022. Printers are network devices. Network devices get hacked.
You think updates are a Microsoft conspiracy. Conspiracy theories do not encrypt files. Ransomware does.
You are still running Windows 7 on a machine that touches the network. Windows 7 is a ghost. Ghosts do not get security patches.
The phrase "I'll update later" is the epitaph of compromised networks. Later never comes. The breach does.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DECLINE THAT WINDOWS UPDATE FOR THE 47TH TIME...

bullets: Hitting the keyboard harder does not make the computer process faster. The keys are not pressure-sensitive accelerators. The computer does not respond to percussive maintenance.

You have cracked the keycap of the Enter key. You have worn the letter 'E' off the keyboard completely. The space bar is sticking because you have compressed the spring with years of aggressive thumb strikes.

"The computer was lagging so I hit it" â€” the computer was lagging because of a network timeout. Hitting it did not resolve the timeout. It just broke the keyboard. Now you need a new keyboard AND a network fix.
Note: A keyboard is an input device, not a punching bag. Aggressive typing does not speed up processing. It just means you type aggressively.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU HAMMER THE KEYBOARD WHEN IT IS SLOW...

bullets: You have been using this keyboard for 3 years. The 'A' key is missing. The 'S' key is missing. The 'Ctrl' key is held on with hope. You have adapted to typing around the gaps. This is not "making do." This is suffering in silence.
"I did not want to bother you" â€” you are bothering me now, with a keyboard that looks like it survived a war. This could have been a 30-second replacement 2 years ago.
The keycaps did not disappear naturally. You pried one off to clean under it, lost it, and never reported it. You have been typing 'A' by stabbing at the exposed switch mechanism.
Note: A keyboard with missing keys is not a "bit of character." It is neglect. Keyboards cost R150. Replace them before they look like dental models of a meth addict.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BRING ME A KEYBOARD WITH MISSING KEYCAPS...

bullets: You spilled coffee on your keyboard. It was working "mostly fine" afterwards, so you did not report it. The sticky residue has now corroded the membrane layer, causing intermittent key registration and random character input.
"It was just a little" â€” it was enough. The sugar in the coffee has crystallised between the layers. The keys are sticking. The keyboard is typing 'kkkkkkkk' every time you press 'k.'
You hid a liquid-damaged keyboard and let it slowly die over 3 months instead of reporting it immediately when it could have been cleaned. Now it is a biohazard.
Note: A keyboard that smells like last week's coffee and types like it is having a seizure is not "still working." It is a health hazard and a productivity disaster.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SPILL LIQUID ON YOUR KEYBOARD AND SAY NOTHING...

bullets: Your custom mechanical keyboard with Cherry MX Blue switches clicks audibly with every keystroke. Every single keystroke. All 80 words per minute of them. The entire office can hear your typing. They hate it.
"I need the tactile feedback" â€” what you need is an awareness that you work in a shared space. The person sitting 3 metres from you can hear every click. They have considered violence.
Open-plan offices are not LAN gaming cafes. Your clack-clack-clack is not impressive. It is hostile. Buy a quiet keyboard or work from home.
Note: A loud mechanical keyboard in an open-plan office is not a productivity tool. It is a declaration of war against your colleagues.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE A LOUD MECHANICAL KEYBOARD IN AN OPEN-PLAN OFFICE...

bullets: The keyboard stopped working because the USB cable has been stretched taught across your desk for 18 months, slowly stressing the internal wires until one finally snapped. This was not sudden. This was gradual and predictable.
You have been eating crisps over this keyboard. There are crumbs under the space bar, between the keys, and inside the switch housings. The crumbs have attracted moisture, which has caused corrosion.
"I did not do anything to it" â€” you did not maintain it. You did not clean it. You did not treat it with care. It failed because of accumulated neglect, not spontaneous mechanical failure.
Note: Keyboards do not "just stop working." They fail because of how they were treated. Every crumb, every stretch, every aggressive keystroke contributed to this moment.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CLAIM THE KEYBOARD 'JUST STOPPED WORKING'...

bullets: You have 200 tabs open across 4 browser windows. The browser is using 8GB of RAM. Your machine has 16GB total. Half of your system memory is dedicated to holding open pages you have not looked at in 3 weeks.

"I will read them later" â€” you will not. The tabs have been open for so long that some of them have logged you out. The pinned tab from 2 months ago is a relic of a task you completed and forgot about.

Each open tab consumes memory, CPU cycles, and your sanity. The browser is not a filing system. It is a temporary viewing window. Close the tabs. Bookmark the ones you need. Revisit them when you actually need them.
Note: A browser with 200 tabs is not "organised." It is a digital hoarding situation that requires intervention.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU KEEP 200 BROWSER TABS OPEN 'FOR REFERENCE'...

bullets: Your to-do list is a collection of 47 open tabs representing tasks you intend to complete. The tabs are not a task manager. They are an anxiety collection. Every open tab is a reminder of something you have not done.
"I keep them open so I do not forget" â€” you will forget anyway. The tabs will blend into the noise of the other 153 tabs. The important task will be buried under cat videos and news articles.

There are applications for task management. They are called "to-do list apps." They are designed for this exact purpose. Your browser tabs are not a productivity system. They are a symptom of avoidance.
Note: Using browser tabs as a memory aid is like writing reminders on toilet paper. Ineffective and destined to be flushed.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE YOUR BROWSER AS A TO-DO LIST...

bullets: Your browser has 200 tabs open, 47 extensions installed, and a cache that has not been cleared since the previous administration. The browser is not slow. It is drowning.
"I only have a few tabs open" â€” you have 4 browser windows with 50 tabs each. You have normalised the chaos. Your perception of "a few" is clinically detached from reality.
The browser is using more memory than your operating system. Chrome's task manager shows that your tabs are consuming resources like a fleet of idling trucks. Close them.
Note: Your browser is not slow. You have given it more work than it can handle. Close some tabs before blaming the software.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU COMPLAIN THAT YOUR BROWSER IS 'TOO SLOW'...

bullets: You have Chrome open with 80 tabs, Firefox open with 60 tabs, and Edge open with 40 tabs. All of them contain the same types of content: research, unfinished tasks, and YouTube videos.
Each browser is independently consuming memory. You have tripled the resource usage for the same set of open tasks. This is not "organising by browser." This is madness.
