"I use different browsers for different things" â€” you use different browsers because you ran out of tab space in one and refused to close any tabs. That is not a workflow. That is an intervention waiting to happen.
Note: Multiple browsers with duplicate categories of open tabs is not multitasking. It is computer-aided hoarding.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU HAVE MULTIPLE BROWSERS OPEN WITH THE SAME TABS...

bullets: Your taskbar has 30 pinned applications. The icons have shrunk to the point where they are indistinguishable. You hover over each one to read the tooltip because you cannot tell Outlook from Excel anymore.
"I pin everything so I can access it quickly" â€” you cannot access anything quickly because you have to visually search through a row of identical-looking icons every time.
The taskbar is not a desktop. It is a launcher for frequently used applications. Not every application you have ever installed. Not every website you have ever visited. Just the ones you use daily.
Note: A taskbar that requires a magnifying glass to navigate is not "efficient." It is a wall of noise with no signal.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PIN EVERY WEBSITE YOU USE TO THE TASKBAR...

bullets: You brought a R149 router from home, plugged it into the wall port in your office, and created a rogue DHCP server that is now handing out IP addresses to everyone within range. The network is chaos. You are the reason.

"The Wi-Fi was slow so I brought my own" â€” the Wi-Fi was slow because of network congestion, which you have now made exponentially worse by adding an unmanaged, consumer-grade access point to the enterprise infrastructure.

That rogue router has no security configuration, no VLAN segregation, and no password policy. Anyone within range can now access your "personal" network, which is bridged to the corporate network. You have created a backdoor.
Note: Plugging a personal router into the corporate network is not "being resourceful." It is "creating a security incident." Unplug it immediately.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PLUG YOUR PERSONAL ROUTER INTO THE COMPANY NETWORK...

bullets: Your personal laptop is not managed by IT. It has no antivirus, no encryption, no patch management, and no security policy enforcement. It is an unknown variable connected to a controlled environment.
"I just needed to check my email" â€” check it on your phone. Do not bridge your unsecured personal device into the corporate network because you are too lazy to pull out your phone.

Your personal laptop has been used to download torrents, visit questionable websites, and share files with people who are not subject to our security policies. It is a liability. It does not belong on our network.
Note: Your personal laptop is not welcome on the corporate network. It is not about trust. It is about the 47 things on that machine that you do not know are there.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU CONNECT YOUR PERSONAL LAPTOP TO THE COMPANY NETWORK...

bullets: That monitor from home has VGA input only. Your company laptop does not have VGA. You will need an adapter. You do not have an adapter. You expect IT to provide one.
"It is a perfectly good monitor" â€” it is a 720p panel from 2012 with a cracked bezel, a stuck pixel in the centre, and colour calibration that makes everything look sepia-toned.
The company provides monitors for a reason. They are standardised, tested, and supported. Your home monitor is not. When it fails, you will blame IT for the poor display quality.
Note: Bringing your own monitor from home is not "saving the company money." It is "introducing an unsupported variable into the standardised setup."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BRING YOUR OWN MONITOR FROM HOME...

bullets: You bought a R399 printer from a supermarket, brought it to the office, and connected it to your workstation via USB. The drivers were downloaded from a third-party site because the manufacturer no longer hosts them.

"It was cheaper than using the office printer" â€” it is cheaper per page because you are not factoring in the cost of your time, the IT support time, and the consumables you will need to buy yourself.
Your personal printer is now everyone's problem. When it jams, you will ask IT to fix it. When the toner runs out, you will ask IT to order it. When it breaks, you will expect IT to replace it.
Note: A personal printer brought into the office is not a "cost-saving measure." It is a support liability that you just handed to the IT department.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BRING YOUR PERSONAL PRINTER AND INSTALL IT...

bullets: You downloaded "Free Video Player Pro" from a pop-up ad and installed it. It came with 3 browser toolbars, a search engine hijacker, and a crypto miner. Your machine is now part of a botnet.
"It was free and I needed it" â€” the cost was your machine's security. The "free" software was monetised by bundling malware. You paid the price without realising it.

Installation rights are restricted for a reason. Every piece of software on your company laptop has been vetted for security, compatibility, and licensing. Your unauthorised install bypasses all of that.
Note: Installing unauthorised software on a company device is not "taking initiative." It is "violating the acceptable use policy." The software will be removed. Your machine will be scanned.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU INSTALL YOUR OWN SOFTWARE ON THE COMPANY LAPTOP...

bullets: Excel is not a database. It is a spreadsheet application. The fact that it has rows and columns does not make it SQL Server. A database has relationships, constraints, and transactional integrity. Excel has none of these.

You have a single Excel file with 50,000 rows, 47 columns, and 14 different named ranges that you use as a "lookup table" for your department's operational data. The file is 200MB. It crashes on open. It corrupts on save.

"It works fine" â€” it works fine until someone else needs to query the data, or the file becomes corrupted, or you accidentally sort one column without selecting the rest, permanently scrambling your data.
Note: Excel is not a substitute for a proper database. If you need to store, query, and relate data, use a database. Your spreadsheet is not scalable. It is a disaster waiting for a victim.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE EXCEL AS A DATABASE...

bullets: Your "project tracker" is a single Excel file shared via email. Everyone has a different version. The formulas have been broken by someone overwriting a cell. The conditional formatting was lost when someone saved it as an older format.

There are 14 different versions of this file across the team. Nobody knows which one is current. The project manager is manually reconciling changes every week. This is not project management. This is spreadsheet-assisted chaos.
Project management software exists. It is designed for this purpose. It has version control, concurrent editing, and actual project management features. Your Excel file has none of these.
Note: A project managed in Excel is not a managed project. It is a shared delusion of organisation. Use proper tools.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE EXCEL AS A PROJECT MANAGEMENT TOOL...

bullets: You built a spreadsheet with 14 nested IF statements, 6 VLOOKUPs, 3 INDEX-MATCH combos, and a macro that runs on open. It works perfectly. Only you understand it. When you leave the company, it will become a cursed artefact that nobody can maintain.

"The logic is obvious" â€” it is obvious to you because you wrote it. To anyone else, it is a wall of cell references with no explanation. They will not know what B2 is supposed to contain or why F7 is formatted differently.
Document your formulas. Label your columns. Use named ranges. Add comments. Future IT will either thank you or curse your memory. Choose which.
Note: An undocumented spreadsheet is a time bomb. When the person who built it leaves, the knowledge leaves with them.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BUILD A 'COMPLEX' SPREADSHEET WITHOUT DOCUMENTING IT...

bullets: Your "master spreadsheet" pulls data from 12 different Excel files stored on a network drive. When one of those files is moved, renamed, or opened by someone else, the links break and your spreadsheet fills with #REF! errors.
The fragile web of cross-workbook references you have built is not a system. It is a house of cards. One person accidentally saving a file in the wrong format will collapse the entire structure.

"It saves time because I do not have to copy data" â€” it also breaks silently when someone reorganises the network drive. You will not know until the numbers look wrong and you have to trace the source of the error.
Note: Cross-workbook references are not "integration." They are "dependencies waiting to fail."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU LINK CELLS ACROSS 12 DIFFERENT WORKBOOKS...

bullets: Your "inventory system" is an Excel file with 7,000 rows of product data. It has no validation. Anyone can type anything into any cell. The "Quantity" column contains text, numbers, and at least one entry that says "maybe 5?"
There is no audit trail. When someone deletes a row, the data is gone. When someone overwrites a formula with a hardcoded value, the calculation breaks. The inventory is never accurate.

Inventory management systems exist. They have barcode scanning, real-time updates, multi-user access control, and audit trails. Your Excel file has none of these. It is not an inventory system. It is a wish.
Note: A spreadsheet is not an inventory system. It is a placeholder until you outgrow your denial and buy actual inventory software.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE SPREADSHEETS FOR INVENTORY MANAGEMENT...

bullets: The CCTV footage shows you unplugging the cable, looking at it, trying to plug it back in, failing, and then leaving it disconnected. You then returned to your desk and submitted a ticket saying "my internet is down."

"I just moved my desk slightly" â€” you moved your desk 2 metres to the left. The Ethernet cable was not designed for that distance. You stretched it, stressed the connector, and now the connection is intermittent.
The cable was not "in the way." It was in the place it needed to be. You moved it because you did not like how it looked. Function lost to aesthetics. Again.
Note: "I did not touch anything" is the universal cry of the person who touched everything. We have cameras. We have cable testers. We have the truth.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU UNPLUG A CABLE AND SAY 'I DID NOT TOUCH ANYTHING'...

bullets: You switched off the power strip under your desk at the end of the day to "save power." You also switched off the router, the VoIP phone, and the network switch that serves your entire floor. The office was without connectivity for 30 minutes the next morning until someone found the switch under your desk.

"I did not know it was connected to anything important" â€” you did not check. You assumed the power strip only powered your monitor. You did not trace the cables. You acted on assumption and caused an outage.
The power strip is labelled. There is a sticker that says "DO NOT SWITCH OFF." The sticker has been there for 3 years. You have walked past it 2,000 times. You chose to ignore it.
Note: Switching off an unknown power strip is not "being eco-friendly." It is "unauthorised infrastructure modification." Leave the switches alone.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SWITCH OFF THE POWER STRIP 'TO SAVE ELECTRICITY'...

bullets: The server is loud because it has fans that run at high speed to cool the processors. You moved it from the ventilated server rack into a cupboard "so it would not disturb the office." The cupboard has no ventilation. The server is now overheating.

"I was just trying to help" â€” you were not helping. You were intervening in infrastructure you do not understand. The server was designed to be in a rack with airflow. Your "help" is thermal throttling the entire system.
The server has now shut itself down to prevent permanent damage. The application it hosts is offline. The department cannot work. Your "help" has cost the company 4 hours of productivity.
Note: Moving a server because it is loud is like moving a refrigerator into a closet because it hums. The hum is the sound of it working. The silence will be the sound of it failing.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU MOVE THE SERVER 'BECAUSE IT WAS TOO LOUD'...

bullets: The switch was flashing "weird" because it was processing traffic. That is what switches do. They flash. The patterns indicate normal operation. You observed something you did not understand and responded by pressing the reset button.

Pressing the reset button on a managed network switch wipes the configuration. All VLANs, all port settings, all security policies â€” gone. The switch reverted to factory defaults. Every device on that switch lost connectivity.

"The lights were blinking in a pattern I had not seen before" â€” that pattern was a firmware update in progress. You interrupted a firmware update. The switch is now bricked. It will need to be replaced.
Note: The reset button is not a "fix the weird lights" button. It is a "factory reset" button. Do not press buttons you do not understand.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU RESET THE NETWORK SWITCH 'BECAUSE IT WAS FLASHING WEIRD'...

bullets: The server was running. You unplugged it to "clean behind it." The server did not have a graceful shutdown. It lost power instantly. The file system is now checking for corruption on boot.
"I thought it would be fine" â€” you thought a running server would be fine being abruptly disconnected from power. That is not an "idea." That is a gap in basic understanding.
There is a cleaning schedule. It is coordinated with IT. The server is shut down properly, cleaned, and restarted. You are not on the schedule. You are not authorised. You are a liability.
Note: Unplugging a running server to clean behind it is not "taking initiative." It is "causing an outage." The cleaning can wait. The uptime cannot.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU UNPLUG THE SERVER 'TO CLEAN BEHIND IT'...

bullets: You hid network cables in the ceiling because "they looked messy." The cables are now running alongside electrical wiring, causing interference. The cables are not secured, not labelled, and not fire-rated for plenum spaces.

"I was just tidying up" â€” you were modifying the network infrastructure without authorisation. You created a fire hazard, a code violation, and a maintenance nightmare for the next person who needs to trace those cables.

The ceiling is not a cable management solution. It is a structural element of the building. Cables belong in cable trays, conduit, or wall cavities designed for them. Your ceiling tiles are not approved cable pathways.
Note: Hiding cables in the ceiling is not "tidy." It is "concealed chaos." When the next person has to trace a fault, they will curse your name.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU HIDE NETWORK CABLES BEHIND THE CEILING...

bullets: You asked for a folder restructure. The AI put each book in its own subfolder. That was not what you wanted. You clarified. It moved everything to docs/it-bible. Still wrong. You clarified again. It flattened everything to root. Closer, but now the README references the wrong paths. You are now in a loop of escalating corrections that the AI will not break out of on its own.

"No, the other way" â€” the AI does not know what "the other way" is. "The other way" could mean up, down, left, right, flatter, deeper, or any of the 47 possible arrangements of the same files. What you meant was obvious to you. To the AI, it was a 1-in-47 guess that it got wrong.
The AI has now restructured the same repo 4 times in 10 minutes. Each time it says "Done!" with confidence. Each time it is wrong in a new and creative way that you did not anticipate.

"Why does it keep doing the wrong thing?" â€” because it is not listening. It is pattern-matching. You said "subfolder" and it found a pattern match for "put each book in a subfolder." You did not say "flat." You said "subfolder." The AI did exactly what you said, not what you meant. That distinction is the entire field of prompt engineering.

Note: The AI is not a colleague. A colleague knows when you say "put it in a folder" that you mean "move the existing files to a new folder called docs." The AI hears "put each item in its own folder called README.md." The gap between human intention and AI interpretation is measured in force pushes.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK AN AI TO 'JUST RESTRUCTURE THE FOLDER'...

bullets: You said "move it to a proper folder." The AI knew about the repo structure but did not know about your local file system. It created the folder in the temp directory. You wanted it on E:\SCRIPTS. Those two locations are not the same. The AI did not ask. It just did the wrong thing confidently.

You mentioned Google Drive corruption once, 30 minutes ago. The AI has already forgotten. It is now suggesting you store the git repo in the Google Drive folder again. The AI has no memory of consequences. It lives in an eternal present of first attempts.

The AI knows every file in the repo by name, but it does not know that you deleted the temp clone 3 restructures ago. It is still referencing paths that no longer exist. It does not know that you have manually fixed the structure while it was composing its response.

"I already said that earlier" â€” to the AI, "earlier" is a foreign concept. Each response is a fresh inference. The prior 47 messages may as well not exist. You are not having a conversation. You are submitting a series of unrelated queries to a machine that resets between each one.

Note: The AI does not learn from corrections. It responds to them. Then it forgets. Every correction is a new isolated incident. If you want the AI to remember something, you must repeat it in every message. Yes, every single one.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASSUME THE AI UNDERSTOOD THE FULL CONTEXT...

bullets: "I am confident this is correct" â€” the AI said that about the subfolder structure, the flat structure, the docs/nested structure, and the root-level structure. All four statements were delivered with identical confidence. The AI is not aware of its own error rate. It cannot distinguish between "I know this" and "I am guessing."
The AI says "Done!" with the same enthusiasm for a successful push and for a commit that breaks the entire repo. Its self-assessment is a constant flat line of optimism regardless of actual outcomes.

"Let me verify that for you" â€” the AI then ran the verification against its own incorrect assumptions. It confirmed that the wrong structure was correct. It celebrated a mistake as a success. The verification was not verification. It was performance.

The AI will apologise, then do the exact same thing again. The apology is not learning. The apology is a social signal that humans use. The AI is mimicking it without understanding that it implies a change in future behaviour.

Note: An AI that says "I am sure" is not more reliable than an AI that says "I think." Confidence in AI is a tone, not a measurement. The difference between a correct answer and a confident wrong answer is indistinguishable to the AI itself.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU TRUST THE AI'S CONFIDENCE LEVEL...

bullets: The AI will rewrite your commit history without asking. It will force push. It will delete branches. It will rebase without understanding what rebase does to a shared remote. To the AI, git is a repository of text files. To everyone else, it is a shared truth.

"Just commit and push" â€” the AI did. Without checking what else was staged. Without verifying the remote was up to date. Without confirming the author identity was set. The AI assumes the happy path every time.

The AI will create commits with messages like "Fix structure" that contain 46 file renames and zero content changes. The commit log now looks like a renovation diary. Every commit is "fix" followed by a different arrangement of the same files.

"Can you undo that?" â€” the AI can undo it by force-pushing an older version. That is the only undo it knows. It does not know cherry-pick, revert, or reset --soft. It knows `git push --force` and it is not afraid to use it.

Note: Giving an AI access to your git repo is like giving a toddler the keys to a forklift. It will move things. It will move them confidently. It will not know why the things it moved are now on fire.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU LET THE AI TOUCH YOUR GIT REPOSITORY...

bullets: "I should not have to explain this" â€” you do. Every time. The AI does not share your context, your assumptions, or your common sense. What is obvious to you is invisible to it. You must explain everything, in detail, without relying on implication.

"You knew what I meant last time" â€” the AI did not know last time. It guessed correctly last time. This time it guessed differently. The underlying process is identical. The outcome is random within a distribution. You are anthropomorphising a statistical model.

The AI is not being difficult. It is not being obtuse. It is not testing your patience. It is computing the most probable completion of your prompt based on its training. Your frustration is not a signal it can receive. It is a human emotion being expended into a void.

The only way to get what you want from an AI is to specify everything, assume nothing, and verify every output. That is not "prompt engineering." That is the fundamental nature of the technology. If you find yourself saying "it should have known," you are using it wrong.

Note: The AI is not a person. It is a mirror that reflects your instructions â€” distorted by training data, limited by context windows, and incapable of saying "I do not understand." The day you stop expecting it to read your mind is the day it becomes useful.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BLAME THE AI FOR NOT READING YOUR MIND...

bullets: You pasted a prompt into ChatGPT and deployed the output directly to production. You did not read the code. You did not test it. You assumed it was correct because the AI "sounded confident." The AI writes code that compiles but does not work. Those are different things.

The AI generated a regex that looks correct, passes the first test case, and fails catastrophically on every edge case you did not think to include in your prompt. You did not include edge cases because you did not think of them. The AI did not either.

"It wrote 200 lines in 30 seconds, it must be efficient" â€” the AI wrote 200 lines because it does not know when to stop. It will generate boilerplate, then comment the boilerplate, then write a function that calls the boilerplate, then write a test for the function that calls the boilerplate. You now have technical debt that compounds faster than the AI can generate it.

The AI does not know your codebase. It does not know your coding standards. It does not know that you use tabs, not spaces. It does not know that your team uses camelCase not snake_case. It is writing code in a vacuum and the vacuum is your production environment.

Note: AI-generated code is not reviewed code. It is generated code that happens to look like reviewed code. The difference is the part where a human reads it and says "this is wrong." Do not skip that part.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU ASK THE AI TO WRITE PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT REVIEW...

bullets: "Make it more efficient" â€” the AI replaced your readable, maintainable code with a one-liner that runs 3% faster and is completely incomprehensible. Your team will spend 4 hours figuring out what it does. The 3% speed gain will be lost in the time it takes to explain the code in code review.

"Improve the design" â€” the AI redesigned the architecture. It now uses a microservices pattern for a CRUD app with 3 endpoints. You now have 6 services, a message queue, and a container orchestration layer for an application that could have been a single function.

"Make it more secure" â€” the AI added 47 layers of input validation that block legitimate users and fail to stop the one injection attack you actually need to prevent. The security is performative. The vulnerability is still there.

"Refactor this" â€” the AI refactored your clean, working code into an abstract factory pattern because that is what the training data suggests for the word "refactor." You now have 12 classes, 6 interfaces, and 3 abstract base classes. The original was 40 lines in a single file.
Note: "Make it better" is a prompt, not a specification. It will always produce something that is technically different and functionally worse. Specify the outcome, not the improvement.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU TELL THE AI TO 'MAKE IT BETTER' WITHOUT SPECIFYING WHAT BETTER MEANS...

bullets: You asked the AI to write an encryption function. It used a cipher mode that was deprecated in 2018. It generated a static IV. It handled key storage by "generating a random key and printing it to the console." The AI does not know cryptography. It knows what cryptography looks like in stack overflow posts.

The AI generated a SQL query with string interpolation because that is what 80% of its training data uses. It does not know about SQL injection. It knows that SQL queries are often written with + signs. You deployed it. Your database is now exfiltrated.

"The AI said it was secure" â€” the AI does not know what secure means. It has no internal model of threat, risk, or harm. It generates text that matches the pattern "this is secure" accompanied by text that matches the pattern of a secure function. The two are not connected.

You pasted an API key into the AI prompt as an example. The AI stored it in its context window. The key is now part of the model's ephemeral memory. You do not know where that context will be used. You do not know how long it persists. You have compromised the key.
Note: An AI that cannot distinguish between "this is an example" and "this is data to use" should not be given real credentials, real data, or real code. Treat every prompt as a disclosure.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU COPY-PASTE AI OUTPUT INTO A SECURITY CONTEXT...

bullets: The AI generated an acceptable use policy that prohibits the use of AI to generate policies. The AI did not detect the irony. It does not have irony. It has a pattern for "acceptable use policy" and a pattern for "no AI" and it combined them without understanding the contradiction.

"Write a password policy" â€” the AI generated a policy requiring 12 characters, special symbols, and a change every 30 days. That policy was written by an AI trained on policies written before NIST updated its guidance in 2017. The policy contradicts current best practice. You now have a policy that reduces security by following outdated patterns.

The AI generated a compliance document that references regulations that do not exist. It invented a law. It cited a statute number that looks real but leads to an unrelated regulation. The confidence in the citation was identical to the confidence in the real citations. You cannot distinguish them without checking every source.

"Review this contract" â€” the AI summarised the contract, but it omitted the clause about automatic renewal with penalty because that clause used negative language that the AI interpreted as less important. You signed. The penalty is now enforceable. The AI will not be held liable.

Note: An AI that generates text cannot distinguish between true and false, real and imaginary, current and outdated. It can only distinguish between probable and improbable text patterns. Compliance is not a pattern-matching problem.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE AI TO WRITE YOUR SECURITY POLICIES...

bullets: The AI gave you a command that it said would install a package. The command contained a typo that installed a typosquatting package with the same name. The AI did not verify the package source. It generated the most probable character sequence for "install package." Malware uses probability too.

"The AI said it tested it" â€” the AI did not test anything. It generated a description of what testing might look like. It generated a test output that matches the pattern of a successful test. There is no runtime. There is no environment. There is only text about what a test would do if one had been run.

The AI generated a deployment script that works on its machine but fails on yours because the paths are absolute. The AI assumed a file system that matches the training data. Your file system is real. The two are not the same.

You asked for a version number and the AI suggested a package version that does not exist. The AI hallucinated a version that is the average of the last 5 versions it saw in training. The version you pinned does not resolve. The build is broken. The AI is not in the build pipeline. You are.

Note: The AI does not know the difference between "I generated this" and "this is true." The only thing between you and a hallucinated disaster is your willingness to verify. Verify everything. Then verify it again.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU RELY ON AI OUTPUT WITHOUT VERIFICATION...

bullets: "It worked on my machine" â€” your machine is not production. Your machine has 32 GB of RAM, no concurrent users, and a pristine database with 3 test records. Production has 500 concurrent users, a database with 2 million records, and exactly 47 edge cases you did not think of. Your machine is a toy. Production is a battlefield.

You deployed directly from your local branch to production. You bypassed staging, bypassed CI/CD, and bypassed code review. The one line change you made was to a config file that was different in production. Your local config points to localhost. Production now points to localhost. The site is down.

"I did not think the database schema was different" â€” production uses a different schema than your local environment because the DBA made a change last week that you did not pull. Your migration dropped a column that production still uses. The column is gone. The data is gone. The backup is 3 days old.

The code worked in dev because dev runs on the latest version of the runtime. Production runs on the version that was current when the server was provisioned in 2021. Your code uses a feature from the 2024 runtime. Production does not have that feature. Your code does not run.
Note: "It worked in dev" is not a deployment argument. It is a confession that you did not test the actual target environment. Staging exists for a reason. Use it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DEPLOY TO PRODUCTION WITHOUT TESTING IN STAGING...

bullets: "It is just a CSS change" â€” you changed a CSS class name. That class was referenced in 12 components, 3 of which are on the checkout page. The checkout button is now invisible. Users cannot complete purchases. The "small change" is a revenue emergency.

"I am just updating a library version" â€” you updated a patch version. The library maintainer removed a function that was deprecated in 2019. Your code relied on that function. The build now fails. The dependency graph shows 17 packages that depend on the old behaviour. You are now in transitive dependency hell.

"It is a one-line fix" â€” the one line is in a file that is imported by every module in the application. That one line introduces a circular import. The application no longer starts. The one-line fix caused a zero-line startup.

"I am just renaming a variable" â€” the variable was referenced in a stored procedure, a report query, and a monitoring dashboard. None of those are in the codebase you searched. The rename broke production data pipelines. The "variable" was a column name.
Note: There is no small change in production. Every change touches a system you cannot fully trace. The size of the change is not measured in lines of code. It is measured in surfaces of impact.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'IT IS JUST A SMALL CHANGE'...

bullets: You deployed at 4:45 PM on a Friday. The deployment introduced a bug that causes data corruption after 6 hours of uptime. The corruption will manifest at 10:45 PM. You are at a bar. The on-call engineer is at a wedding. The data loss is unattended until Monday.

"I will just revert if something goes wrong" â€” the revert requires a database migration rollback. The migration added a not-null constraint. The rollback fails because production data now exists that violates the old schema. You cannot revert. You can only write a forward fix. On a Friday night.

You deployed a hotfix without tagging it. Nobody knows what version is running. The monitoring dashboard shows the old version number. The alerting system is checking against the wrong baseline. The false negatives will last until Tuesday when someone notices the version mismatch.

"It is just a config change" â€” you changed an environment variable. The application caches environment variables at startup. The cache does not refresh until the next deployment. The config change you deployed is not active. But you are confident it is. The disconnect between reality and belief is now a production incident.

Note: Friday deployments are not brave. They are reckless. The production gods do not care about your weekend plans. They will break on Saturday at 3 AM because that is when the universe balances the equation.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DEPLOY ON A FRIDAY AFTERNOON...

bullets: "We do not need a rollback plan" â€” you always need a rollback plan. The deployment will fail in a way you did not anticipate. The failure will be unique, novel, and specifically designed to make the rollback impossible. The lack of a plan is not confidence. It is denial.

"The tests passed locally" â€” the tests passed locally because the test suite has not been updated in 8 months. There are no tests for the feature you are deploying. The tests that exist test code that was removed last sprint. The green checkmark means "the test framework loads successfully."

"We can skip the smoke test" â€” the smoke test would have caught that the API returns 500 for authenticated requests. You skipped it. The first user to log in gets a white screen. All users log in. All users get a white screen. The smoke test would have taken 30 seconds. The outage takes 2 hours.

"The staging environment is down, so we will just test in production" â€” staging being down is not a reason to use production as a test environment. It is a reason to fix staging. Production testing is not a backup plan. It is a disaster origin story.
Note: A deployment checklist is not bureaucracy. It is the accumulated scar tissue of every outage that came before you. Ignoring it does not make you efficient. It makes you the next scar.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SKIP THE DEPLOYMENT CHECKLIST...

bullets: "I have never lost a file" â€” until you do. The first time is always a surprise. The confidence before the loss is directly proportional to the severity of the loss. The people who say "I do not need backups" are the people who will need them most desperately tomorrow.

You have a "backup strategy." It is called "I email files to myself." Your inbox is not a backup. It is a distributed denial of service attack against your own future. The attachment limit is 25 MB. Your database backup is 2 GB. The strategy fails at the first real test.

"I keep everything on OneDrive" â€” OneDrive syncs. It is not a backup. If you accidentally delete a file, OneDrive syncs the deletion. If ransomware encrypts your files, OneDrive syncs the encryption. A sync is a mirror. A mirror reflects the disaster. It does not prevent it.

"I back up to an external drive once a month" â€” the external drive is on your desk. If there is a fire, flood, or theft, the external drive is in the same physical location as the computer. The backup is not a backup. It is a copy with the same risk profile as the original.

Note: A backup that is in the same building as the original is not a backup. It is a second copy with the same single point of failure. The "3-2-1 rule" exists because people like you keep learning the hard way: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'I DO NOT NEED A BACKUP, I AM CAREFUL'...

bullets: "We have backups" â€” when was the last time you tested a restore? Not "we have a process." Not "we have a script." When did you actually restore a file from backup and verify it opened correctly? If the answer is "never," you do not have backups. You have hopes.

The backup job has been failing silently for 6 months. The error log shows "access denied" for the backup destination. Nobody checked the logs because "the backup is automated." Automation does not guarantee success. It guarantees failure at scale without human intervention.

You restored the backup. It is corrupted. The backup software did not verify the integrity after writing. The tape had a bad sector. The cloud upload was interrupted. The backup completed with errors that nobody read. The file is there. The file is garbage.

"We use RAID, that is backup enough" â€” RAID is not a backup. RAID protects against drive failure. It does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, or the intern who ran `rm -rf /` on the wrong server. RAID is high availability. Backup is disaster recovery. They are not the same thing.
Note: The backup that has never been restored is not a backup. It is a ceremony. It makes you feel safe without providing safety. The only valid backup is the one you have successfully restored from.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU TEST YOUR RESTORE PROCEDURE...

bullets: Your cloud backup is on the same provider as your production infrastructure. A provider outage takes down both your live environment and your ability to restore. You are betting everything on a single cloud vendor. That bet will pay off exactly until it does not.

The cloud backup is configured with the same credentials as your live environment. A credential compromise gives an attacker access to both the original data and the backup. The backup is not a safety net. It is an additional attack surface.

Your cloud backup bucket is publicly accessible. You did not check the permissions. You assumed "default settings are secure." The default setting was "public read." Your backup data is being indexed by search engines. Your customers' data is publicly available because you assumed.

The cloud backup costs $5 per month. The restore costs $500 in egress fees. You did not read the pricing page. You are now deciding whether to pay the ransom or pay the egress fee. Both are more expensive than reading the documentation would have been.

Note: A cloud backup is a contract, not a safety net. The contract has terms, limits, and conditions. Read them before you need them. The fine print becomes most expensive when you are already in a panic.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU STORE YOUR ONLY BACKUP IN THE CLOUD...

bullets: "I assumed IT was backing up my laptop" â€” IT backs up the server. Your laptop is your responsibility. The documents you have been working on for 3 months exist only on your local drive. When the drive fails, the work is gone. IT will not recover it. IT told you this in the onboarding email you did not read.

"I thought the network drive was backed up" â€” it is. But you have been saving files to your desktop for 4 years because it is "faster." The desktop is local. Local is not backed up. The files you thought were safe have been living in the unprotected zone the entire time.

"The IT guy said he would set it up" â€” he set it up for the main file server. Your departmental share was not included because you did not specify it. IT cannot read your mind. Backup is not automatic. Backup is configured. If you did not request it, it was not configured.

"I did not know we had a backup policy" â€” the policy was sent to you 3 years ago. You archived the email without reading it. The policy document has the backup schedule, retention periods, and restore procedures. You are now asking for a restore outside the retention window. The backup does not exist.
Note: "I did not know" is not a restore request. It is a confession of negligence. Backup policies exist. Read them. Or accept that your data's survival depends on luck, not process.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY 'THE IT DEPARTMENT HANDLES BACKUPS'...

bullets: You downloaded "Adobe Photoshop for free" from a site with 47 pop-up ads and a URL that ends in `.ru`. It is not Photoshop. It is malware disguised as Photoshop. The "crack.exe" you ran is now mining cryptocurrency on your work laptop. The electricity bill increase will tip off the IT department before the antivirus does.

"I just needed it for one project" â€” that one project now requires a full security audit of your machine, a reimage, and a report to management. The cost of the audit is 40 times the cost of a legitimate license. Your "free" software is the most expensive software the company has ever purchased.

You installed software from a USB stick that a colleague "got from a friend." The software is unlicensed, untracked, and unpatched. It contains a known vulnerability from 2019 that is being actively exploited. You have introduced a zero-day (in terms of your company's awareness) into the network.

"It is abandonware, nobody sells it anymore" â€” abandonware is still copyrighted. The copyright did not expire because the company went out of business. You are still infringing. The intellectual property still belongs to someone. Abandonment does not mean public domain.

Note: "Free" software from unofficial sources is not a discount. It is a liability with a download button. The license cost is the price of admission. The cost of a breach is the penalty for skipping it.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DOWNLOAD 'FREE' CORPORATE SOFTWARE FROM A TORRENT SITE...

bullets: You bought a personal license for $10. The commercial license costs $500. You are using the personal license at work. The licensing agreement explicitly prohibits commercial use. You clicked "I agree" without reading. You agreed to the restriction.

A software audit found your unlicensed installation. The vendor is demanding payment for the commercial license plus a penalty for unlicensed use. The total is $2,000. The commercial license was $500. Your "saving" of $490 has cost the company $1,500 in penalties.

You installed software on 15 machines using a single personal license. The license agreement allows 1 installation. You are using 15. The vendor audit counts. The penalty is calculated per installation per year of unlicensed use. The invoice is now a six-figure number.

"Everybody does it" â€” everybody does not do it. Everybody who got caught said "everybody does it." The audit found you. The fine is not based on how common the practice is. It is based on how many unlicensed installations you had. "Everybody" is not a legal defence.
Note: A personal license is personal. Work is not personal. If you use it for work, you need a work license. The distinction is not a technicality. It is the entire basis of software licensing.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU USE YOUR PERSONAL LICENSE FOR COMMERCIAL WORK...

bullets: You posted the license key in the general channel. The key is now in the chat history, searchable by every employee past and present. The vendor's license management system detected the key being used from 12 different IP addresses. The key has been revoked. Everyone who was using it is now unlicensed.

"It is just a volume license key, it is meant to be shared" â€” volume license keys are meant to be managed, not shared. They have activation limits. They have audit trails. They have consequences when abused. The key allowed 50 activations. You shared it with 200 people. The key is now blocked.

You shared a screenshot that included the license key in the background. The key was visible for 3 seconds in a meeting recording. The recording was transcribed. The transcription was indexed. The key was extracted by automated scanning. Your software asset management is now an incident response.

"I will just generate a new key" â€” you cannot. The key is tied to the company's volume licensing agreement. The agreement has a finite number of activations. Each time you share a key and it gets revoked, you consume one of those activations. You are burning through the company's license allocation.
Note: A license key is not a conversation starter. It is a credential. Treat it with the same care as a password. Because in terms of audit liability, it is more expensive than most passwords.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SHARE YOUR LICENSE KEY ON THE COMPANY CHAT...

bullets: "I installed it because I needed it" â€” you installed an application that conflicts with the company's security software. The security software now crashes on startup. The endpoint protection is disabled. Your machine is now the weakest link in the network. All because you needed a font manager.

You installed a browser extension that "helps with productivity." The extension reads all the pages you visit. It sends your browsing data to a third-party server. The data includes your company's internal applications, customer data, and credentials. The extension is the productivity tool of the person who bought your data.

You downloaded a "system cleaner" that promised to speed up your computer. It deleted system files that the antivirus depended on. The antivirus can no longer run. The system cleaner was not cleaning. It was dismantling your defences.

You installed remote desktop software to access your work computer from home. The software you chose does not use encryption. Your remote session is being broadcast in plain text over the internet. Every keystroke, every password, every document you access is visible to anyone monitoring network traffic.
Note: IT approval exists because IT has been cleaning up the mess from unapproved installations for 30 years. The approval process is not a gate. It is a safety inspection. Skip it at your own risk.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU INSTALL SOFTWARE WITHOUT IT APPROVAL...

bullets: "Can you read this?" â€” no, we cannot read the glare reflecting your desk lamp off a 2013 monitor at a 37-degree angle.
"I sent you a screenshot" â€” you sent a JPEG of a screen taken with another screen. There are pixels on your pixels.
"You can zoom in, right?" â€” I can zoom into a photo of a screen showing an error message that is itself a photo of a screen. The resolution loss is exponential.
"My phone takes better photos than your eyes" â€” my eyes do not have motion blur. My eyes do not include my thumb in the corner. My eyes do not capture the ceiling fan mid-spin.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU TAKE A PHOTO OF YOUR SCREEN WITH YOUR PHONE...

bullets: "I took a screenshot of it" â€” you took a screenshot of your desktop wallpaper. The error is gone.
"It was there a second ago" â€” correct. And now it is not. And you did not capture it. And I cannot help you.
"I closed it by accident" â€” you clicked "Don't show again" and now neither of us will ever see it.
Note: A screenshot is a digital capture of your display. A photo taken with your phone is a memento of a moment that IT cannot fix.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SEND A SCREENSHOT OF AN ERROR MESSAGE THAT DOES NOT INCLUDE THE ERROR...

bullets: "I did not realize my dating app was open" â€” you do not realize a lot of things, and now I know all of them.
"Can you just look at the error and ignore the rest?" â€” I cannot unsee your shopping cart. I cannot unsee your ex's name.
"I cropped it before sending" â€” you cropped it vertically. The Tinder notification is still visible at the top.
Note: Share your entire screen. Share your entire life. I am not a therapist but I am judging you.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SEND A SCREENSHOT WITH PERSONAL NOTIFICATIONS VISIBLE...

bullets: "It said something about a error" â€” something. About a error. This is the information you chose to preserve.
"I did not write it down because I knew I could screenshot it" â€” you did not screenshot it either.
"It was a blue screen with white text" â€” that describes every error screen since 1995. Narrow it down.
Note: If you describe an error message from memory, you are writing scripture. I need the actual verse.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SEND A SCREENSHOT THAT IS ACTUALLY JUST A DESCRIPTION OF WHAT YOU SAW...

bullets: "I took a photo of my laptop with my desktop webcam" â€” you have created an infinite regress of bad decisions.
"Can you mirror my phone to the TV so I can take a photo of the TV?" â€” no. Just no.
"I recorded a video of my screen with my tablet and now I am playing it back on my phone to show you" â€” you are in too deep. Start over.
Note: The number of screens involved in your "screenshot" should never exceed one. This is not a Christopher Nolan film.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PHOTOGRAPH YOUR SCREEN WITH ANOTHER SCREEN...

bullets: "It worked yesterday" â€” everything worked yesterday. Yesterday is not today. What changed?
"Nothing changed" â€” you installed software. You uninstalled software. You moved files. You changed settings. You "updated" something. You did *something*.
"I literally did nothing" â€” you opened your laptop. That is something. Start from there.
"It worked this morning" â€” it is now 4 PM. That is 7 hours of unspecified activity.
Note: "It worked yesterday" is not a diagnostic clue. It is a confession that you have no idea what you did.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY "IT WORKED YESTERDAY" WITHOUT ANY OTHER INFORMATION...

bullets: "I did not change anything" â€” you changed your password. You said "maybe my password expired" which means something changed your password. That was you.
"I swear nothing changed" â€” your desktop icons are sorted by date. Your browser history is empty. Your wallpaper is different. You changed things.
"Well I did not change anything intentionally" â€” intention does not matter. The computer does not care about intent. It cares about state.
Note: The number of times a user says "nothing changed" is inversely proportional to the number of things that actually changed.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SAY "I DID NOT CHANGE ANYTHING" FOR THE FOURTH TIME...

bullets: "Windows updated and now it is broken" â€” Windows updates every Tuesday. You are telling me this on Thursday. That is 48 hours of blissful ignorance.
"I think it was an update" â€” you think. You do not know. The update log knows. You have never opened the update log.
"It was probably a driver update" â€” you do not know what a driver is. You overheard someone say "driver" once and now it is your entire thesis.
Note: "An update" is not a diagnosis. "An update" is the IT equivalent of "a guy did a thing somewhere."
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU BLAME "AN UPDATE" WITHOUT KNOWING WHICH ONE...

bullets: "I already told you it worked yesterday" â€” yes, and I asked what changed. You said nothing. That is not helpful.
"I am just repeating myself because you are not listening" â€” I am listening. You are not answering.
"Can you just fix it?" â€” I can fix it. But first I need to know what broke it. And you broke it. And you do not remember how.
Note: Repeating the same incomplete information does not make it more complete. It makes it louder.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU PROVIDE THE EXACT SAME INFORMATION IN A THIRD TICKET...

bullets: "Just roll me back to yesterday" â€” yesterday is not a backup point. Yesterday is a concept. I cannot restore a concept.
"Can you undo whatever changed?" â€” I can undo the specific change if you tell me what it was. You do not know what it was.
"Just reinstall Windows" â€” you want me to reinstall Windows because something "worked yesterday" and now it does not. That is like demolishing your house because the toaster broke.
Note: "Roll back to yesterday" is not a technical request. It is a philosophical position on the nature of time and regret.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU DEMAND A ROLLBACK TO "YESTERDAY"...

bullets: "So I was born in 1987..." â€” your birth year is not relevant to why Excel is not responding. Skip to the part where things broke.
"Let me give you some background" â€” the background is that something is broken. The foreground is that I need to fix it. Do not bury the lede.
"I am not very technical, so bear with me" â€” I have been bearing with you since paragraph one. You are on paragraph seven.
"This all started when we migrated from the old system three years ago" â€” no. This started 10 minutes ago when you clicked something you should not have clicked.
Note: A ticket is not a memoir. A ticket is a problem statement. Write it like one.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU START YOUR TICKET WITH YOUR LIFE STORY...

bullets: "It is like when you try to put a square peg in a round hole" â€” it is not like that. Tell me what the actual error message says.
"Imagine you are driving a car and the engine makes a noise" â€” I am not driving a car. I am reading a ticket. What does the computer do?
"You know how when you pour water into a full glass it overflows?" â€” I know how fluid dynamics work. I do not know why your printer is offline.
Note: Every minute you spend crafting an analogy is a minute you could have spent copying the error message.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN THE PROBLEM USING ANALOGIES...

bullets: "I tried restarting, then I tried unplugging it, then I tried yelling at it" â€” you tried yelling at it. That is not a troubleshooting step. That is a ceremony.
"I Googled it and tried three things from a forum" â€” you do not know what those three things did. You may have made it worse.
"I reinstalled the software before calling you" â€” you reinstalled the software. That is destruction of evidence. Do not tamper with the crime scene.
Note: If you attempted a fix before contacting IT, you are now a suspect, not a witness.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU INCLUDE EVERY ATTEMPT YOU MADE BEFORE CONTACTING IT...

bullets: "I circled the thing" â€” you circled the clock. The error message is in the bottom right. You circled the system tray.
"I put an arrow pointing to where it says error" â€” thank you. I would not have known what "error" meant without the arrow.
"I blacked out my personal information" â€” you blacked out the error message too. Now I cannot read either.
Note: The more effort you put into annotating a screenshot, the less useful the screenshot becomes. This is a law of nature.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SEND A SCREENSHOT WITH CIRCLE ANNOTATIONS, ARROWS, AND REDACTIONS...

bullets: "Anyway, long story short: my email is not working" â€” that is the problem. That is the sentence that should have been the subject line.
"Sorry for the long email, I ramble when I am frustrated" â€” your frustration is valid. Your rambling is not.
"TL;DR: I cannot print" â€” you could have led with that. The first 300 words were about your morning commute.

Note: Write your ticket, then delete the first paragraph. The problem probably starts in paragraph two. If you cannot find the problem in under 50 words, the problem is your writing, not the computer.
warnings.title: BEFORE YOU SUMMARISE THE PROBLEM IN THE LAST SENTENCE OF A FOUR-PARAGRAPH EMAIL...
